wrong_choices: Those who take God's name in vain by swearing, cursing, and lying by it | Those who despise preaching and God's Word and will not hear it gladly | Those who openly bow down to images and worship false gods as the heathen do
basis_note: Psalm 31:6 sets clinging to worthless idols against trusting the LORD, and 2 Kings 17:9 says the Israelites secretly did wrong against the LORD by building high places.
audit_why: Three wrong choices were really the same as the catechism's answer, so they were replaced with open idolatry and sins against the Second and Third Commandments, and the right choice now reads "love, fear, and trust".

question: Whom do all idolaters really serve?
answer: They serve the devil who is the father of lies, and the lord of all impenitent and hardened sinners
right_choice: They serve the devil, father of lies and lord of hardened sinners
wrong_choices: They serve the holy angels, messengers of God and helpers of believers | They serve only themselves, lovers of self and lords of their own lives | They serve the Lord God, unknowingly, Father of all and Lord of all people
basis_note: Pagan sacrifices are offered to demons (1 Cor 10:20), Jesus calls the devil the father of lies (John 8:44), and whoever practices sin is of the devil (1 John 3:8).
audit_why: Three wrong choices named the devil, Satan or demons, so they were also right; they were replaced with clearly wrong choices, and 1 Cor 10:20-21 was added as the reference. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer draws on three passages together (idolaters serve demons, the devil is the father of lies, and the devil is lord of those who keep sinning), but the reference cited only 1 Cor 10:20-21, which alone does not support the whole answer, so the reference is corrected to include John 8:44 and 1 John 3:8 as well.

question: What does God require of us in the first commandment?
answer: We should fear, love, and trust in God above all things
right_choice: We should fear, love, and trust in God above all things
wrong_choices: We should not misuse God's name but call upon it in trouble | We should honor and obey our parents and other authorities | We should keep the day of rest holy and gladly hear God's Word
audit_why: The answer is the catechism's own teaching, but two wrong choices only reworded "fear, love, and trust", so they were replaced with requirements of other commandments, and a Bible reference was added.

question: Upon what does God really look?
answer: Upon the attitude of our hearts toward Him
right_choice: Upon the attitude of our hearts toward Him
wrong_choices: Upon our perfect keeping of the commandments | Upon our outward obedience and good deeds | Upon the words we speak and vows we make
basis_note: The LORD contrasts outward appearance, which man sees, with the heart, which the LORD sees. The answer's "attitude of our hearts toward Him" is a fuller statement of "the heart."
audit_why: The catechism's answer (God looks at the heart) is right and fits 1 Samuel 16:7, so I added that reference and removed the word "then", which only made sense after an earlier question.

question: When do we fear God?
answer: We fear God when we think so highly of Him, that we are afraid of offending Him by any wrongdoing
right_choice: We fear God when we think so highly of Him we fear offending Him
wrong_choices: We fear God when we expect every good thing from Him and turn to Him in every need | We fear God when we gladly listen to His Word and give thanks for all His gifts | We fear God when we are so afraid of His punishment that we try to hide from Him
basis_note: Proverbs 14:2 ties fearing the LORD to walking in uprightness rather than devious ways, and Psalm 89:7 shows God as greatly feared and awesome above all, matching the high regard in the answer.
audit_why: The three wrong choices only restated the right answer, so they were also correct; they are now replaced with the catechism's other ideas (trusting God, terror of punishment, thankfulness) that are not what fearing God means.

question: Of how many kinds is the fear of God?
answer: Of two kinds: slavish fear and child-like fear
right_choice: Of two kinds: slavish fear and child-like fear
wrong_choices: Of two kinds: natural fear and spiritual fear | Of two kinds: fear of God and fear of punishment | Of three kinds: fear, love, and trust
basis_note: No shown verse counts kinds of the fear of God. Job 31:23 shows terror at God's calamity and Psalm 103:13 shows fear as a child's relation to a father, but neither says there are two kinds.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What is meant by slavish fear?
answer: When we fear God because we are afraid of punishment
right_choice: When we fear God because we are afraid of punishment
wrong_choices: When we fear God because we want to obey His will | When we fear God because we love Him and do not want to offend Him | When we respect God for His power and divine majesty
basis_note: 1 John 4:18 says fear involves punishment and is driven out by perfect love, so the answer, fearing God out of dread of punishment, follows from the verse. The phrase "slavish fear" itself does not appear.
audit_why: One wrong choice ("He is mighty and just") could pass for fear of punishment, so it was replaced with the childlike fear of love, and 1 John 4:18 was added as a reference.

question: What is meant by child-like fear?
answer: When we love God so dearly that we wish to do nothing that is against His will
right_choice: When we love God so dearly that we wish to do nothing against His will
wrong_choices: When we fear God's punishment and avoid all wicked actions | When we honor God with our lips while our hearts are far from Him | When we tremble at God's voice and obey His commands
basis_note: 1 John 5:3 says the love of God is keeping His commandments, and Genesis 22:12 shows fear of God as not withholding what He asks, so the answer follows from these verses.
audit_why: One wrong choice (respecting God as children respect their parents) is almost the same as child-like fear, so it was replaced with a clearly wrong choice about empty lip-service.

question: Who fear God in this manner?
wrong_choices: Only those who have reached a certain level of spiritual maturity | All people, regardless of their relationship with God | Those who fear God's authority without truly loving Him
basis_note: No shown verse says only God's children fear Him this way. Psalm 103:13 and Proverbs 14:26 link fearers with God's compassion and their children, while Psalm 34:11 invites children to learn the fear of the LORD.

audit_why: No fault found.

question: When do we love God?
answer: We love God when He is dearer to us than all else, so that we have no true joy except in Him, and gladly submit to His will in all things
right_choice: God is dearer to us than all, we have joy only in Him, gladly submit to His will
wrong_choices: We love God when we fear His punishment and so avoid open sin | We love God when we are grateful for His gifts always | We love God when we attend church and confess our sins
basis_note: The answer is the catechism's own gloss on the First Commandment. 1 John 5:3 supports only the part about keeping God's commandments; the shown verses do not say God is dearer than all else or that joy is found only in Him.
audit_why: One wrong choice spoke of keeping God's commandments, which the Bible also calls love for God, so it was replaced with a choice that is clearly not the catechism's teaching.

question: According to 1 John 2:15, if anyone loves the world, what is not in him?

basis_note: 1 John 2:15 says that if anyone loves the world, "the love of the Father is not in him," which matches the printed answer.

question: Why must we love God?
answer: We must love God because of His goodness toward us
right_choice: We must love God because of His goodness toward us
wrong_choices: We must love God because of His power and majesty | We must love God to earn our salvation | We must love God to escape His punishment

question: Whereby is it seen that we love God?

question: When do we trust in God above all things?

wrong_choices: When we obey His commandments and do what He requires | When we pray and ask God for help in our troubles | When we have faith that He will answer all our prayers

question: Why must we trust in God alone?
answer: Because He is our almighty and faithful Friend

question: What is meant by the "name" of God?
answer: The names given to Him in the Bible, and everything by which He makes Himself known, such as His Word and His works.

question: When is the name of God taken in vain?

question: What is it to curse by the name of God?

question: What is it to swear by the name of God?

question: Are we ever permitted to swear an oath?

question: Why is it a great sin to commit perjury?

question: What is it to conjure by the name of God?

wrong_choices: Speaking God's name carelessly in anger or in ordinary talk | Teaching false doctrine and claiming that God has taught it | Attempting to perform miracles through prayer and invoking God's power to heal diseases

question: How do we lie and deceive by the name of God?

question: Why must we honor father and mother?

question: How are children to show that they honor father and mother?

question: What is the duty of parents toward their children?

question: What is it to steal?

audit_why: Two wrong choices were so close to the catechism's four means that they could also seem right, so they were replaced with clearly wrong ones, and a reference was added.

question: If a poor Creature comes to Christ, crying, lamenting and confessing his sins, will Christ receive him?
answer: YES, YES: His merciful Arms are spread wide open to receive him
right_choice: YES, YES: His merciful Arms are spread wide open to receive him
wrong_choices: Yes, but he must prove his sincerity through works of righteousness first. | Only if his confession is heard and accepted by a priest or minister of the church. | Yes, but only after proper penance and restitution have been made by the penitent sinner.
basis_note: John 6:37 says that the one who comes to Christ, He will never drive away, so the answer yes follows from it. Matthew 11:28 invites the weary and burdened to come to Him. The arms image is illustration, not in the text.
audit_why: The catechism's answer is right (Jesus says He will never drive away the one who comes to Him), so I added the references John 6:37 and Matthew 11:28 and corrected the spelling "mercifull" to "merciful".

question: What will the Lord do for such a one that comes to him?
answer: 1. He will Pardon all their sins. 2. He will give them Grace. 3. He will give them Peace. 4. He will Comfort them. 5. He will provide for them. 6. He will take their parts. 7. He will bring them to Heaven
right_choice: He will pardon their sins, grant them grace and peace, comfort them, provide for them, and bring them to Heaven
wrong_choices: Pardon them immediately and sanctify them completely so they need not struggle against sin. | Accept them into His church but delay their eternal rewards until they prove themselves worthy. | Grant them prosperity and protection from earthly troubles, health, and a long and comfortable life.
reference: Romans 4:8; Psalms 85:8; Isaiah 30:18; Isaiah 30:19; Psalms 135:14; Deuteronomy 28:12; 2 Timothy 4:18
verses: Romans 4:8; Psalms 85:8; Isaiah 30:18; Isaiah 30:19; Psalms 135:14; Deuteronomy 28:12; 2 Timothy 4:18
basis_note: Romans 4:8 gives pardon, Psalms 85:8 peace, Isaiah 30:18-19 grace and an end to weeping, Psalms 135:14 vindication, Deuteronomy 28:12 blessing, and 2 Timothy 4:18 the heavenly kingdom; the list is drawn from these together.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: When the Lord has done this for a poor Creature, what must he do for this good God of his?
answer: He must be Humble and Thankful
right_choice: He must be Humble and Thankful
wrong_choices: He must be Strong and Steadfast in faith | He must be Holy and Righteous always | He must be Patient and Obedient forever
basis_note: Psalm 116:12-13 answers the question of how to repay the Lord's goodness with thankful praise and calling on His name; Isaiah 66:2 names the humble and contrite in spirit as the one God esteems.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: How must he show himself humble and thankful?
answer: He must love the Lord with all his heart, with all his soul, and serve the Lord with all his strength, and he must love his neighbor as himself, for the Lord's sake; and this he must do all the days of his life.
right_choice: Love the Lord with all your heart and soul, and love your neighbor as yourself all the days of your life
wrong_choices: Fast and pray often, attend worship every week, and give a tenth of your income to the Lord. | Thank God daily in prayer, avoid all sin in thought and action, and keep yourself pure. | Give generously to the poor, serve others humbly, and live a life of self-denial.
basis_note: Luke 10:27 says to love the Lord with all the heart, soul, and strength, and to love one's neighbor as oneself. The answer's "serve" and "for the Lord's sake" are its own wording, not in the verse.
audit_why: One wrong choice (obeying God's commandments) is nearly the same as loving God and neighbour, so it was replaced, and the missing reference to Matthew 22:37-39 was added. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer's phrase "with all his strength" comes from Luke 10:27, not Matthew 22:37-39, so the reference needed to include Luke 10:27 as well; the choices themselves were fine against the fuller passage set.

question: Who made you?
wrong_choices: My parents | Nature | Society
basis_note: Psalm 100:3 says outright, "It is He who made us, and we are His," so the answer God is stated. Genesis 1:27 supports it by recording that God created man.
audit_why: The answer "God" is right, but the question had no Bible reference, so I added Genesis 1:27 and Psalm 100:3, which say God made us.

question: What else did God make?
wrong_choices: God made only the things we can see | God made only the plants and animals | God made only the things in heaven
basis_note: Colossians 1:16 says all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, and Genesis 1:1 says God created the heavens and the earth. Together they teach that God made all things.
audit_why: Each wrong choice was also true (God did make the heavens and earth and living creatures, and "except evil" is nearly the same as "all things"), so they were replaced with clearly wrong "only" choices, and a reference (Gen 1:1; Col 1:16) was added.

question: Why did God make you and all things?
wrong_choices: To test mankind's obedience | To establish His kingdom | For man's happiness
basis_note: Isaiah 43:7 says God's people were "created for My glory," which states the answer directly. Revelation 4:11 supports it by ascribing glory to God as Creator of all things.
audit_why: The answer matches the catechism and the Bible (people are "created for My glory," and God created all things), but the question had no reference, so Isaiah 43:7 and Revelation 4:11 were added.

question: How can you glorify God?
answer: By loving him and doing what he commands.
right_choice: By loving him and doing what he commands.
wrong_choices: By studying theology and philosophy | By being rich and respected in the world | By doing whatever seems right to us
basis_note: 1 Corinthians 10:31 calls us to do everything for God's glory, and 1 John 5:3 says the love of God is keeping His commandments. Together they teach the answer.
audit_why: Two wrong choices (avoiding sin and doing good works; attending church and praying) are really ways of obeying God, so they were replaced with clearly wrong ones, and a reference was added. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The reference Col 3:17 doesn't support the 'loving him' part of the answer; 1 John 5:3 does, so the reference was corrected to 1 Cor 10:31; 1 John 5:3.

question: Why ought you to glorify God?
answer: Because he made me and takes care of me.
right_choice: Because he made me and takes care of me.
wrong_choices: Because it makes us happy | Because He will reward those who obey | Because the Church requires it
basis_note: Psalm 100:3 says the LORD made us and we are His people and the sheep of His pasture. "Made" is stated; the shepherd image teaches that He cares for us.
audit_why: The catechism answer is right and matches Psalm 100:3, but the question had no Bible reference, so Ps 100:3 was added.

question: Are there more gods than one?
In how many persons does this one God exist?
wrong_choices: In countless manifestations | In seven spiritual forms | In two persons
basis_note: At Jesus's baptism the Son is baptized, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks; 2 Corinthians 13:14 names the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the Holy Spirit together. The count of three persons follows from these.
audit_why: The catechism answer (three persons) is right, but the question had no reference, so I added Matthew 3:16-17 and 2 Corinthians 13:14, where Father, Son and Holy Spirit appear together.

question: What are they?
answer: The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
right_choice: The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
wrong_choices: The Father, the Son, and the Angel Gabriel | The Power, the Love, and the Wisdom of God | The Father, the Son, and the Virgin Mary
basis_note: Matthew 28:19 names the three persons outright: baptizing "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." Matthew 3:16-17 shows all three present at Jesus' baptism.
audit_why: The answer used the old "Holy Ghost" wording, so it now says "Holy Spirit" as in the BSB; one wrong choice (Creator, Redeemer, Sanctifier) could also be right, so it was replaced; and a reference was added.

question: What is God?
answer: God is a Spirit, and has not a body like men.
right_choice: God is a Spirit, and has not a body like men.
wrong_choices: God is a great man who lives in heaven. | God is an angel who rules over the other angels. | God is a force in nature that has no mind or will.
basis_note: John 4:24 says plainly that "God is Spirit." The denial of a body like men is not stated there but follows from calling God Spirit.
audit_why: The question had no reference (John 4:24 now added), and the wrong choices were either true of God or too close to "Spirit", so they were replaced with clearly wrong ones.

question: Where is God?
wrong_choices: God is only in heaven, far above the earth | God is present only in holy places | God is only in the hearts of believers
basis_note: Psalm 139:7-10 says no place escapes God's presence: heaven, Sheol, the farthest sea. Jeremiah 23:24 agrees that He fills heaven and earth.
audit_why: Two wrong choices were partly true (God is in heaven and dwells in believers), so they now say "only," which the Bible contradicts, and a reference to Psalm 139 and Jeremiah 23:24 was added.

question: Can you see God?
answer: No; I cannot see God, but he always sees me.
right_choice: No; I cannot see God, but he always sees me.
wrong_choices: No; I cannot see God, and he sees me only when I pray | Yes, in our thoughts and dreams | Yes, when you look at creation
basis_note: John 1:18 says no one has ever seen God. Hebrews 4:13 says nothing in creation is hidden from God's sight, so he sees everything, including us.
audit_why: One wrong choice ("No, but He speaks to us through conscience") could also be picked since it starts with "No", so it was replaced with one that contradicts God always seeing us, and a Bible reference (John 1:18; Hebrews 4:13) was added.

question: Does God know all things?
answer: Yes; nothing can be hid from God.
right_choice: Yes; nothing can be hid from God.
wrong_choices: Yes, only the important matters | Yes, but not our free choices | Yes, but not the future
basis_note: 1 John 3:20 says God "knows all things," and Hebrews 4:13 says nothing in all creation is hidden from His sight, which matches the answer's "nothing can be hid from God."
audit_why: The catechism answer is right and the wrong choices are clearly wrong, but the question had no Bible reference, so I added Hebrews 4:13 and 1 John 3:20.

question: Can God do all things?
answer: Yes; God can do all his holy will.
right_choice: Yes; God can do all his holy will.
wrong_choices: No; some things are too hard even for God. | Yes; God can do whatever people ask of him. | No; God can do only what is easy.
basis_note: Job 42:2 says God can do all things and no plan of His can be thwarted; Psalm 115:3 says He does as He pleases. The answer's "holy will" wording is a reasonable reading of these.
audit_why: The wrong choice "except what is contrary to His nature" was nearly the same as the catechism's answer, so I replaced the vague wrong choices with clearly wrong ones in the same style and added Ps 115:3 and Matt 19:26 as references. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and wrong choices are sound, but the reference should cite Job 42:2 along with Ps 115:3, since Job 42:2 ("I know that You can do all things") is the primary verse behind the catechism's answer; Matt 19:26 is replaced since it wasn't among the verses specified as holding this answer.

question: Where do you learn how to love and obey God?
wrong_choices: In the Bible and Church tradition | In philosophy and human reason | In the teachings of wise men
basis_note: Paul says all Scripture is God-breathed and useful for training in righteousness, so that the man of God is equipped for every good work. The answer follows from these verses.
doubt: The verses say Scripture trains in righteousness and equips for good works, but they do not say "alone," which goes slightly beyond the text.
audit_why: The catechism's answer is right and its wrong choices are fair, but the question had no Bible reference, so 2 Timothy 3:16-17 was added.

question: Who wrote the Bible?
answer: Holy men who were taught by the Holy Ghost.

question: Who were our first parents?
wrong_choices: Noah and his wife | Abraham and Sarah | Cain and Abel
basis_note: Genesis 4:1 says Adam had relations with his wife Eve and she bore Cain. Genesis 3:20 names Eve as the mother of all the living, so Adam and Eve are the first parents.
audit_why: The answer is right and the choices are fair, but the question had no Bible reference, so I added Genesis 2:7, 21-22 and 3:20.

question: Of what were our first parents made?
answer: God made the body of Adam out of the ground, and formed Eve from the body of Adam.
right_choice: God made the body of Adam out of the ground, and formed Eve from the body of Adam.
wrong_choices: God formed both Adam and Eve from the dust of the ground | God created Adam and Eve in the same manner from the earth | God made Adam from the ground, and formed Eve from the animals He had made
basis_note: Genesis 2:7 says the LORD God formed the man from the dust of the ground, and Genesis 2:22 says He made the woman from the rib taken from the man.
audit_why: The catechism answer matches Genesis 2, but the question had no reference and one wrong choice (Eve from the sky) was unbelievable, so I added the reference and replaced that choice with a more believable wrong one.

question: What did God give Adam and Eve besides bodies?
answer: He gave them souls that could never die.
right_choice: He gave them souls that could never die.
wrong_choices: He gave them angels to be their servants. | He gave them gold from the land of Havilah. | He gave them wings to fly above the earth.
basis_note: Genesis 2:7 says God breathed the breath of life into Adam and he became a living being. It does not mention a soul or say that it could never die; that is church teaching on the soul's immortality.
doubt: The shown verses do not support "could never die." Genesis 3:19 speaks of returning to dust, and Genesis 3:22 implies Adam could have lived forever only by eating from the tree of life, which suggests he was not created with unending life.
audit_why: Three wrong choices described things that are also true of people (spirits returning to God, love, reason and free will), so they were replaced with clearly wrong ones, and Gen 2:7 was added as the reference.

question: Have you a soul as well as a body?
answer: Yes; I have a soul that can never die.
right_choice: Yes; I have a soul that can never die.
wrong_choices: Yes, but my soul will perish at death | Yes, my soul is my mind and will | Yes; my soul will enter another body when I die
basis_note: Matthew 10:28 distinguishes soul from body and says men cannot kill the soul, so the soul outlives the body's death. It does not say the soul can never die.
doubt: Matthew 10:28 says God can destroy both soul and body in hell, and Ezekiel 18:4 says the soul who sins will die, so "can never die" goes beyond these verses.
audit_why: One wrong choice (the soul comes from God and returns to Him) is also true in Scripture, so it was replaced with a clearly wrong idea, and Matthew 10:28 was added as the reference.

question: How do you know that you have a soul?
answer: Because I can think about God and the world to come.
right_choice: Because I can think about God and the world to come.
wrong_choices: Because I can see, hear, and feel with my body. | Because I can eat, drink, and grow each day. | Because I can walk, run, and play with others.
basis_note: No shown verse says that thinking about God and the world to come proves a soul. 1 Corinthians 2:11 only says a man's thoughts are known to the spirit within him, which is close but not the stated argument.
audit_why: The catechism's answer is kept, but the wrong choices also described the soul, so they were replaced with things that belong to the body and are the same length as the right answer.

question: In what condition did God make Adam and Eve?
answer: He made them holy and happy.
right_choice: He made them holy and happy.
wrong_choices: He made them sinful and in need of a Savior | He made them perfect in all knowledge | He made them strong and wealthy
basis_note: God saw all He had made and called it very good (1:31), and blessed Adam and Eve and gave them dominion (1:28). Holiness and happiness are drawn from this, not stated in these words.
doubt: The shown text says "very good" and records God's blessing, but never uses the word "holy"; the answer's "holy" goes beyond these verses.
audit_why: Two wrong choices were also true (being innocent and without sin, and being able to choose good or evil), so they were replaced with clearly wrong ones, and Genesis 1:26-31 was added as the reference.

question: What is a covenant?
answer: An agreement between two or more persons.
right_choice: An agreement between two or more persons.
wrong_choices: A gathering of people for worship | A law established by divine authority | A promise made by God to mankind
basis_note: Laban proposes to Jacob, "let us make a covenant, you and I," and God makes a covenant with Israel including those not present, showing a covenant as an agreement between parties.
audit_why: One wrong choice, "A bond created by mutual consent," says nearly the same thing as the catechism's answer, so I replaced it with a choice that is clearly wrong.

question: What covenant did God make with Adam?
wrong_choices: The covenant of grace | The covenant of obedience | The Mosaic covenant
basis_note: God gives Adam a command with a condition: eat freely, but eating from the tree brings death. Hosea 6:7 says Israel, like Adam, transgressed the covenant, so the arrangement is called a covenant. "Covenant of works" is a theological label drawn from these verses.
audit_why: The catechism's answer, the covenant of works, is right, but the question had no reference, so I added Genesis 2:16-17, where God commands Adam and warns of death. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The reference was missing Hosea 6:7, the verse that actually calls God's dealing with Adam a 'covenant'; it has been added alongside Gen 2:16-17.

question: What was Adam bound to do by the covenant of works?
wrong_choices: To offer sacrifices for sin | To trust in a promised Savior | To repent and be forgiven
basis_note: God commands Adam to eat freely of the garden but not from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, on pain of death. Adam is bound to keep that command; Hosea 6:7 says he transgressed the covenant.
audit_why: Three wrong choices were also true of Adam's duty (loving God, keeping the commandments, working the garden), so they were replaced with things that belong to the covenant of grace or to fallen people, and the reference Gen 2:16-17 was added.

question: What did God promise in the covenant of works?
answer: To reward Adam with life if he obeyed him.
right_choice: To reward Adam with life if he obeyed him.
wrong_choices: To give Adam's children a land forever | To forgive Adam if he repented of sin | To save Adam through a promised Savior
basis_note: God commands Adam to eat freely of the garden but not from the tree of knowledge, warning that he will surely die. The promise of life for obedience is implied by that warning, not stated outright.
audit_why: Two wrong choices were nearly the same as the catechism's answer of life for obedience, and the third was true elsewhere in Genesis, so all three were replaced with clearly wrong choices, and the reference Genesis 2:16-17 was added.

question: What did God threaten in the covenant of works?
answer: To punish Adam with death if he disobeyed.
right_choice: To punish Adam with death if he disobeyed.
wrong_choices: To remove Adam's dominion over creation | To cause Adam great suffering and pain | To cast Adam out of the garden
basis_note: God told Adam that eating from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil would bring death: "in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die."
audit_why: The question and answer match Genesis 2:17 ("you will surely die"), but the question had no Bible reference, so Gen 2:16-17 was added.

question: Did Adam keep the covenant of works?
wrong_choices: Yes; he obeyed God in everything | Yes; only Eve broke God's command | Yes; he kept it until he died
basis_note: Adam ate the forbidden fruit (Gen 3:6), and God says he ate from the tree He had commanded him not to eat (Gen 3:17), so Adam disobeyed God rather than keeping the covenant.
audit_why: The wrong choices all described Adam's sin and so were also true, so they were replaced with choices saying he kept the covenant, and the Genesis 3 reference was added.

question: What is meant by want of conformity?
answer: Not being or doing what God requires.
right_choice: Not being or doing what God requires.
wrong_choices: Not knowing what God has said. | Being tempted to do wrong. | Doing what God forbids.
basis_note: Psalm 78:10 describes people who failed to keep God's covenant and refused His law (doing), and Acts 8:21 says a heart "not right before God" (being). Together they teach the answer.
audit_why: The three wrong choices all said almost the same thing as the right answer, so I replaced them with choices that are clearly different: transgression (doing what God forbids), ignorance, and temptation.

question: What is meant by transgression?
wrong_choices: Being born with a sinful nature | Being punished for our sins | Not doing what God requires
basis_note: Transgression is breaking God's covenant by doing what He forbids: Israelites who worship other gods are transgressing His covenant, "which I have forbidden." Daniel 9:11 likewise says Israel "transgressed Your law."
audit_why: Two of the wrong choices were just other ways of saying "doing what God forbids", and the third was too close to it, so they now give clearly different ideas, including the catechism's own contrast, "not doing what God requires".

question: What was the sin of our first parents?
Who tempted them to this sin?
answer: The devil tempted Eve, and she gave the fruit to Adam.

question: What befell our first parents when they had sinned?
answer: Instead of being holy and happy, they became sinful and miserable.

question: Did Adam act for himself alone in the covenant of works?
answer: No; he represented all his posterity.
right_choice: No; he represented all his posterity.
wrong_choices: No; he acted as a priest for mankind | No; he represented all creation | No; he represented only those who would believe
basis_note: Romans 5:18-19 says one man's trespass brought condemnation for all, and his disobedience made the many sinners, so Adam's act bound all his posterity. The words "covenant of works" are not in the verses.
audit_why: The question had no Bible reference, so Romans 5:12-19 was added. One vague wrong choice ("God acted through him") could also be called true, so it was replaced with a clearly wrong one.

question: What effect had the sin of Adam on all mankind?
answer: All mankind are born in a state of sin and misery.
right_choice: All mankind are born in a state of sin and misery.
wrong_choices: All mankind are born in a state of grace and favor. | All mankind are born in a state of neutrality and freedom. | All mankind are born in a state of innocence and peace.
basis_note: Romans 5:12 says death passed on to all men because all sinned, and Romans 5:19 says through one man's disobedience the many were made sinners. Together they teach the sin and misery in the answer, though "born" is an inference.
audit_why: The three wrong choices were all true results of Adam's sin (Romans 5:12), so they were replaced with choices that are clearly wrong, and the reference Romans 5:12 was added. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and wrong choices match the catechism and are supported by Romans 5:12 and 5:19 together, so the reference was expanded to include both verses.

question: What is that sinful nature which we inherit from Adam called?
wrong_choices: The unpardonable sin | Sin of omission | Actual sin
basis_note: Romans 5:12 says death passed to all because all sinned through Adam, and Psalm 51:5 says the psalmist was sinful from conception. The inherited sinful condition is taught there, though the term "original sin" itself does not appear.
audit_why: The three wrong choices were all other ways of saying "original sin", so they were replaced with different kinds of sin, and Romans 5:12 was added as the reference. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and wrong choices are correct, but the reference should also include Psalm 51:5, which the catechism uses to teach this doctrine, so it was added.

question: What does every sin deserve?
answer: The wrath and curse of God.

question: Can any one go to heaven with this sinful nature?
answer: No, our hearts must be changed before we can be fit for heaven.
right_choice: No, our hearts must be changed before we can be fit for heaven.
wrong_choices: Yes, God's mercy and grace can forgive all of our sins completely | No, we must perform good works to earn righteousness and fitness first | No, only those whom God predestined before creation can enter heaven
basis_note: Jesus says no one can see or enter the kingdom of God unless born again of water and the Spirit, since flesh is born of flesh and spirit of the Spirit. The answer's need for a changed heart follows from this new birth.
audit_why: The question and answer fit the teaching that we must be born again (John 3:3-7), but it had no reference, so John 3:3-7 was added.

question: What is a change of heart called?
wrong_choices: Justification | Sanctification | Adoption
basis_note: Jesus says no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again, and John 3:5-7 adds birth of water and the Spirit. The word "regeneration" itself does not appear, but the new birth it names is taught there.
audit_why: "Conversion" is so close in meaning to a change of heart that it could also be chosen, so it was replaced with "Adoption", and the reference John 3:3-7 (being born again) was added.

question: Who can change a sinner's heart?
wrong_choices: God the Father alone | Jesus Christ alone | A faithful pastor
basis_note: Jesus says no one enters God's kingdom unless born of the Spirit; flesh gives birth only to flesh, and the new birth is by the Spirit, as the wind moves where it wishes.
audit_why: The answer matches the catechism and John 3, where new birth is the work of the Spirit, but the question had no reference, so John 3:5-8 was added.

question: Can any one be saved through the covenant of works?
answer: None can be saved through the covenant of works.
right_choice: None can be saved through the covenant of works.
wrong_choices: Those who are baptized can be saved through the covenant of works | Some can be saved through the covenant of works | Only the children of Abraham can be saved through the covenant of works
basis_note: Galatians 3:10-11 says those who rely on works of the law are under a curse and that no one is justified before God by the law, so the law-works route saves no one.
audit_why: Two wrong choices ("those who obey" and "the righteous") could be called true in principle, since the law promises life to those who keep it perfectly, so they were replaced, and Galatians 3:10-11 was added as the reference.

question: Why can none be saved through the covenant of works?
answer: Because all have broken it, and are condemned by it.
right_choice: Because all have broken it, and are condemned by it.
wrong_choices: Because it was made with Adam in the garden | Because Christ replaced it with the covenant of grace | Because it was given only to the Jews at Sinai
basis_note: Romans 3:23 says all have sinned, so all have broken the law. Galatians 3:10 says everyone who relies on works of the law is under a curse, which is the condemnation the answer describes.
audit_why: One wrong choice (perfect obedience required) is itself a true reason none can be saved by works, so it was replaced with a clearly wrong one, and the reference to Romans 3:23 and Galatians 3:10 was added.

question: With whom did God the Father make the covenant of grace?
wrong_choices: With Abraham, the father of faith | With Moses, the lawgiver of Israel | With his prophets and priests
basis_note: 2 Timothy 1:9 says grace was given us in Christ Jesus before time began, which points to a pre-temporal arrangement centered on the Son. The verse never uses the word covenant or names the parties.
audit_why: One wrong choice ("all believers in Christ") is close to the fuller teaching that the covenant is in Christ for his people, so it was replaced, and the reference 2 Timothy 1:9 was added.

question: Whom did Christ represent in the covenant of grace?
wrong_choices: The faithful and righteous | All who hear the gospel | The Jewish nation only
basis_note: Hebrews 9:15 calls Christ the mediator of the new covenant so that "those who are called" receive the eternal inheritance, and He died to redeem them. The verse says "called," not "elect," so "elect" is the catechism's doctrinal term for those people.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What did Christ undertake in the covenant of grace?
answer: To keep the whole law for his people, and to suffer the punishment due to their sins.
right_choice: To keep the law for his people and suffer the penalty for sins
wrong_choices: To show his people the law and set them an example to follow | To give a new law to his people and help them keep it | To set aside the law for his people and forgive sins without penalty
basis_note: Galatians 4:4-5 says Christ was born under the law to redeem those under the law, and Hebrews 9:15 says he died to redeem them from their transgressions. Together these teach both parts of the answer.
audit_why: The three wrong choices all described Christ's work in nearly the same words as the catechism's answer, so I replaced them with choices that clearly differ from keeping the law and bearing the penalty for his people.

question: Did our Lord Jesus Christ ever commit the least sin?
answer: No; he was holy, innocent and undefiled.
right_choice: No; he was holy, innocent and undefiled.

audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: One of the listed reference verses, Isa 9:5, does not speak to Christ's divine nature as the answer requires; it has been corrected to Isa 9:6, which does, while the rest of the reference and all answer choices remain accurate.

question: But who is that Mediator who at the same time is true God and a true and righteous man?
answer: Our Lord Jesus Christ, who became to us wisdom from God—our righteousness, holiness, and redemption.
right_choice: Our Lord Jesus Christ, who became to us wisdom from God, our righteousness, holiness, and redemption
wrong_choices: The greatest human teacher who lived righteously and demonstrated the path to God | The Holy Spirit given by God to provide wisdom and sanctification to believers | God the Father, who made all things and provides wisdom and redemption alone
basis_note: 1 Corinthians 1:30 names Christ Jesus as our wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and redemption; 1 Timothy 2:5 calls him the mediator, "the man Christ Jesus"; 1 John 5:20 says he is the true God.
audit_why: The answer quoted 1 Corinthians 1:30 in non-BSB wording ("sanctification", "whom God made"), so it now follows the BSB ("holiness", "who became to us wisdom from God"), and that verse is added to the references. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and wrong choices are fine, but the reference listed passages (Matt 1:21-23; Luke 2:11) that don't actually establish Christ as Mediator who is true God and true man, so the reference was corrected to the verses that do: 1 Cor 1:30; 1 Tim 2:5; 1 John 5:20.

question: From where do you know this?
answer: From the holy gospel, which God Himself first revealed in Paradise. Later, He had it proclaimed by the patriarchs and prophets, and foreshadowed by the sacrifices and other ceremonies of the law. Finally, He had it fulfilled through His only Son.
right_choice: From the gospel: God revealed it in Paradise, proclaimed by patriarchs and prophets, foreshadowed in the law
wrong_choices: From personal experience and the wisdom of great men about how to find salvation | From the New Testament alone, which replaced the Old Testament and all its ancient prophecies | From the reasoning of Greek philosophers about the nature of God and man
basis_note: The answer rests on the verses: God first promised the woman's seed in Paradise (Gen 3:15), spoke through the prophets and then through His Son (Heb 1:1-2), and the law's sacrifices were a shadow of the good things to come (Heb 10:1).
audit_why: One wrong choice spoke of ancient prophets predicting the Messiah, which is also part of the catechism's answer, so I replaced it with a choice about Greek philosophers that is clearly wrong.

question: Are all men, then, saved by Christ just as they perished through Adam?
answer: No. Only those are saved who by a true faith are grafted into Christ and accept all His benefits.
right_choice: No. Only those are saved who by a true faith are grafted into Christ and accept all His benefits.
wrong_choices: Only those who have been baptized and properly received the church sacraments are truly saved | Yes, because Christ died for all humanity and therefore all people are saved through His death | No, some are saved by faith in Christ while others are saved by their good works
basis_note: Only those who believe have eternal life, while those who reject the Son remain under God's wrath. Believers are grafted in and stand by faith, while unbelieving branches were broken off.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: According to the Heidelberg Catechism, what is true faith?
answer: True faith is a sure knowledge whereby I accept as true all that God has revealed to us in His Word. At the same time it is a firm confidence that not only to others, but also to me, God has granted forgiveness of sins, everlasting righteousness, and salvation, out of mere grace, only for the sake of Christ's merits. This faith the Holy Spirit works in my heart by the gospel.
right_choice: Sure knowledge of God's Word and firm confidence that Christ's merits save me by grace
wrong_choices: A feeling, produced by my own will, that God is pleased with me | Knowing that God exists, even as the demons believe, without personal trust in Him | A hope that God will forgive me if my good works outweigh my sins
basis_note: Hebrews 11:1 defines faith as assurance and certainty, Romans 3:24 says we are justified freely by grace through Christ, and Romans 10:17 says faith comes by hearing the word of Christ.
audit_why: The catechism's answer is right, but "True/False" cannot answer "What is true faith?", so I gave a short form of the catechism's answer and three believable wrong choices.

question: What, then, must a Christian believe?
answer: All that is promised us in the Gospel, which the articles of our catholic and undoubted Christian faith teach us in a summary.
right_choice: All promised in the Gospel, which the articles of Christian faith teach in summary
wrong_choices: Only those teachings of the apostles which are clearly and directly written in the Bible | What the church has determined and declared to be necessary for all true Christians | Whatever brings personal comfort and hope based on our individual understanding of Scripture
basis_note: John 20:31 says the gospel record is written so you may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life; Galatians 3:22 ties the promise to faith in Christ. The creed summary is church teaching.
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The reference (Matt 28:19) did not actually support the answer; it is replaced with John 20:30-31 and Galatians 3:22, which do.

question: In the Apostles' Creed, how do we confess that Jesus Christ was conceived and born?
answer: He was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary.
right_choice: He was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary.
wrong_choices: Conceived by Joseph, born of the virgin Mary | Conceived by the angel Gabriel, born of Elizabeth | Conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of Joseph's wife Elizabeth
audit_why: The original answer was the whole Creed with stray numbering, and its choices were vague, overlapping lists; the question now asks about one article of the Creed, which Matthew 1:20-23 confirms, with clear wrong choices.

question: How are these articles divided?
answer: Into three parts: the first is about God the Father and our creation; the second about God the Son and our redemption; the third about God the Holy Spirit and our sanctification.
right_choice: Into three parts: God the Father and creation; God the Son and redemption; God the Holy Spirit and sanctification
wrong_choices: Into various parts based on each sacrament and how it individually applies to believers | Into two main parts: the teachings of the Old Testament and the New Testament faith | Into ten parts, one for each of the Ten Commandments and corresponding doctrine
basis_note: No shown verse divides the creed into three parts. This threefold arrangement (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) is the catechism's own teaching, though passages like 1 Peter 1:2 and 1 Corinthians 8:6 name the same persons.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Since there is only one God, why do you speak of three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?
answer: Because God has so revealed Himself in His Word that these three distinct persons are the one, true, eternal God.
right_choice: Because God revealed in His Word that these three distinct persons are the one, true God
wrong_choices: Because the three persons represent different roles that God plays in salvation | Because human minds cannot comprehend one God, so we use three | Because the Father is God, but the Son and Spirit are not divine
basis_note: No verse states the answer outright, but together these verses teach it: the LORD is one (Deut 6:4), the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ are each named as the one God (1 Cor 8:6), and the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit share one "name" (Matt 28:19).
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The catechism answer and wrong choices are sound against these verses, but the reference list was overloaded and oddly formatted, so it was trimmed to the three verses (Matt 28:19; Deut 6:4; 1 Cor 8:6) that actually hold the answer.

question: What do you believe when you say: I believe in God the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth?
answer: That the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who out of nothing created heaven and earth and all that is in them, and who still upholds and governs them by His eternal counsel and providence, is, for the sake of Christ His Son, my God and my Father. In Him I trust so completely as to have no doubt that He will provide me with all things necessary for body and soul, and will also turn to my good whatever adversity He sends me in this life of sorrow. He is able to do so as almighty God, and willing also as a faithful Father.
right_choice: The eternal Father of Christ, Creator of all, who upholds all, is my God and Father in whom I trust
wrong_choices: God the Father is the Creator of all things, but it is Christ who upholds them | God the Father created all things long ago, but may not provide for our daily needs | The eternal Father has power over creation, but we should primarily trust our own ability
basis_note: Gen 1:1, Ps 104:27-30 and Eph 1:11 show God creating, sustaining and governing all things; Rom 8:15-16, Matt 6:30, Rom 8:28, Gen 18:14 and Matt 7:9-11 show His fatherly care, power and good purpose. "Out of nothing" is inferred, not stated.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What do you understand by the providence of God?
answer: God's providence is His almighty and ever present power, whereby, as with His hand, He still upholds heaven and earth and all creatures, and so governs them that leaf and blade, rain and drought, fruitful and barren years, food and drink, health and sickness, riches and poverty, indeed, all things, come not by chance but by His fatherly hand.
right_choice: God's almighty power by which He upholds all things and governs all creatures by His fatherly hand
wrong_choices: God's saving power by which He redeems His people and brings them safely to heaven | God's judging power by which He punishes the wicked and rewards the righteous in this life | God's creative power by which He made all things and then left them to run by themselves
basis_note: Scripture teaches that the Son upholds all things by His powerful word, that not a sparrow falls apart from the Father's will, that the lot's every decision is from the LORD, and that God gives rain and fruitful seasons.
audit_why: Two wrong choices (sovereign decree, foreknowledge) and "creative power that sustains" were so close to the catechism's answer that they could also be chosen, so I replaced them with clearly different ideas (God leaving creation alone, saving power, judging power).

question: What does it benefit us to know that God has created all things and still upholds them by His providence?
answer: We can be patient in adversity, thankful in prosperity, and with a view to the future we can have a firm confidence in our faithful God and Father that no creature shall separate us from His love; for all creatures are so completely in His hand that without His will they cannot so much as move.
right_choice: We can be patient in adversity, thankful in prosperity, and confident no creature shall separate us from His love.
wrong_choices: We can be patient in adversity, thankful in prosperity, and assured that God's love remains certain if we are faithful. | We should be patient in adversity, obey God in prosperity, and demonstrate through our faithfulness that we truly trust Him. | We can be patient in adversity, thankful in prosperity, and demonstrate our righteous standing before God through our sincere obedience.
basis_note: Job 1:21-22 shows patience in loss, Deuteronomy 8:10 calls for thanks in plenty, Romans 8:38-39 says nothing can separate us from God's love, and Job 1:12 and Proverbs 21:1 show creatures under God's hand.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Why is the Son of God called Jesus, that is, Saviour?
answer: Because He saves us from all our sins, and because salvation is not to be sought or found in anyone else.
right_choice: Because He saves us from all our sins, and salvation is found in Him alone
wrong_choices: Because He was born in Nazareth, where Joseph and Mary made their home | Because the priests chose the name for Him at the temple in Jerusalem | Because He teaches us the way and example of how to live righteously before God
basis_note: Matthew 1:21 says the Son will save His people from their sins, and Acts 4:12 says salvation exists in no one else, covering both parts of the answer.
audit_why: Two wrong choices (His punishment-bearing and resurrection, and His ransom) also describe how Jesus saves, so they could be picked fairly; they were replaced with choices that clearly do not explain the name in Matthew 1:21.

question: Do those believe in the only Saviour Jesus who seek their salvation and well-being from saints, in themselves, or anywhere else?
answer: No. Though they boast of Him in words, they in fact deny the only Saviour Jesus. For one of two things must be true: either Jesus is not a complete Saviour, or those who by true faith accept this Saviour must find in Him all that is necessary for their salvation.
right_choice: No, they deny that Jesus is the complete Saviour in whom all necessary salvation must be found
wrong_choices: Yes, because saints may add what is lacking in what Jesus has done for salvation | Yes, provided they also trust their own good works for part of their salvation | Yes, since they still confess Jesus with their lips as their Saviour and Lord
basis_note: Christ holds all God's fullness, and believers are made complete in Him, while those seeking justification elsewhere are severed from Christ, so seeking salvation outside Him denies Him as Saviour.
audit_why: The three wrong choices all said "No" with reasons that were also true, so they were replaced with clearly wrong "Yes" answers; the question and answer are unchanged.

question: Why is He called Christ, that is, Anointed?
answer: Because He has been ordained by God the Father, and anointed with the Holy Spirit, to be our chief Prophet and Teacher, who has fully revealed to us the secret counsel and will of God concerning our redemption; our only High Priest, who by the one sacrifice of His body has redeemed us, and who continually intercedes for us before the Father; and our eternal King, who governs us by His Word and Spirit, and who defends and preserves us in the redemption obtained for us.
right_choice: As God's anointed, He is our Prophet revealing God's will, our Priest who redeemed us through sacrifice, and our eternal King
wrong_choices: As God's anointed, He is our Lawgiver like Moses, our Priest offering sacrifices yearly, and our King over Israel alone | As God's anointed, He is our Judge condemning sinners, our Scribe interpreting the law, and our Commander of armies | As God's anointed, He is our Prophet foretelling coming events, our Priest of the line of Aaron, and our earthly King
basis_note: God anoints Him with the Spirit and above His companions (Ps 45:7; Isa 61:1), and the verses show Him as prophet (Deut 18:15), priest forever (Ps 110:4), and eternal king (Luke 1:33).
audit_why: The catechism's answer is sound, but the wrong choices were close synonyms of Prophet, Priest and King and only the right one echoed 'anointed', so I gave all choices the same opening and made the wrong ones clearly contrary to the teaching.

question: Why are you called a Christian?
answer: Because I am a member of Christ by faith and thus share in His anointing, so that I may as prophet confess His Name, as priest present myself a living sacrifice of thankfulness to Him, and as king fight with a free and good conscience against sin and the devil in this life, and hereafter reign with Him eternally over all creatures.
right_choice: Because I am a member of Christ by faith and share His anointing as prophet, priest, and king
wrong_choices: Because I attend church regularly and participate in its sacraments faithfully | Because I believe in the teachings of Christ and live a moral life | Because Christ called His followers Christians during His earthly ministry to them
basis_note: Believers are members of Christ's body (1 Cor 12:27), share His anointing (1 John 2:27), are a royal priesthood (1 Pet 2:9), fight the devil (Eph 6:11), and reign with Him (2 Tim 2:12).
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Why is He called God's only begotten Son, since we also are children of God?
answer: Because Christ alone is the eternal, natural Son of God. We, however, are children of God by adoption, through grace, for Christ's sake.
right_choice: Because Christ alone is God's eternal natural Son, while we are children of God by adoption through grace
wrong_choices: Because Christ is God's Son by adoption through grace, while we are God's children by nature from birth | Because Christ is the only One born of God, while all believers become God's children at baptism | Because Christ became God's Son at His baptism, while we are God's children by nature through creation
basis_note: Christ is the one and only Son who is God and was with God in the beginning, while believers are predestined for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, by grace in the Beloved.
audit_why: Two wrong choices were close to the catechism's own teaching (children of God through Christ's work, or through faith), so I replaced them with choices that clearly contradict it.

question: Why do you call Him our Lord?
answer: Because He has ransomed us, body and soul, from all our sins, not with silver or gold but with His precious blood, and has freed us from all the power of the devil to make us His own possession.
right_choice: Because He ransomed us, body and soul, from sin and the devil's power with His precious blood
wrong_choices: Because He taught us God's law, so that by keeping it we earn freedom from sin and the devil | Because He has authority over us as our supreme Master and demands our obedience and worship | Because He rewarded us for our good works, body and soul, with silver and gold and a place in heaven
basis_note: Peter says we were redeemed with the precious blood of Christ, not silver or gold; Hebrews says He freed us from the devil's power; Paul says we were bought at a price, so we are not our own.
audit_why: Two wrong choices described being bought, freed from darkness, or owned by creation, which are also true, so they were replaced with choices that clearly contradict the catechism's teaching of redemption by Christ's blood.

question: What do you confess when you say: He was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary?
answer: The eternal Son of God, who is and remains true and eternal God, took upon Himself true human nature from the flesh and blood of the virgin Mary, through the working of the Holy Spirit. Thus He is also the true seed of David, and like His brothers in every respect, yet without sin.
right_choice: The eternal Son of God took on true human nature from the virgin Mary through the Holy Spirit, remaining true God, without sin
wrong_choices: The Son of God took true human nature from the virgin Mary through the Holy Spirit, but ceased to be God | The Son of God became human born of the virgin Mary to demonstrate that sinless living is always possible | Jesus received human nature from both Mary and Joseph, and became the Son of God only at His birth
verses: John 1:1; John 1:14; Luke 1:35; Romans 1:3; Hebrews 2:17; Hebrews 4:15
basis_note: The Word who was God (John 1:1) became flesh (John 1:14) through the Holy Spirit's coming upon Mary (Luke 1:35), a descendant of David (Romans 1:3), made like His brothers yet without sin (Hebrews 2:17; 4:15).
audit_why: Two wrong choices were also acceptable (one said the same thing as the right answer, another was close to "God with us"), so they were replaced with choices that clearly contradict the catechism and the Bible.

question: What benefit do you receive from the holy conception and birth of Christ?
answer: He is our Mediator, and with His innocence and perfect holiness covers, in the sight of God, my sin, in which I was conceived and born.
right_choice: He is our Mediator and with His innocence and perfect holiness covers my sin before God
wrong_choices: His innocent life shows us that sinless living is possible and teaches us how to overcome temptation | His holy birth and innocent life give us an example of perfect obedience and moral purity to imitate | His conception and birth in purity remove our guilt and enable us to become holy ourselves
basis_note: Christ is the one mediator between God and men (1 Tim 2:5). The sinless One was made sin for us so we might become God's righteousness (2 Cor 5:21). Psalm 51:5 shows the sin we were conceived in.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What do you confess when you say that He suffered?
answer: During all the time He lived on earth, but especially at the end, Christ bore in body and soul the wrath of God against the sin of the whole human race. Thus, by His suffering, as the only atoning sacrifice, He has redeemed our body and soul from everlasting damnation, and obtained for us the grace of God, righteousness, and eternal life.
right_choice: That Christ bore God's wrath against the sin of humanity, and through His suffering as atoning sacrifice redeemed us
wrong_choices: That Christ experienced all our pain and sorrow to show His sympathy with our struggles and sorrows | That Christ bore all our sicknesses and pain so we could be physically and spiritually healed | That Christ suffered greatly throughout His life to show us how to endure persecution and hardship faithfully
basis_note: Isaiah 53:5 and 53:10 show the Servant bearing our punishment as a guilt offering; 1 Peter 2:24 says He bore our sins in His body; 2 Corinthians 5:21 gives righteousness; 1 John 2:2 gives atonement for the whole world.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Why did He suffer under Pontius Pilate as judge?
answer: Though innocent, Christ was condemned by an earthly judge, and so He freed us from the severe judgment of God that was to fall on us.
right_choice: Though innocent, Christ was condemned by an earthly judge, freeing us from God's severe judgment
wrong_choices: Christ was sentenced by human authority to teach us that obedience to God matters most | Christ was condemned by an earthly court to show us that innocent people sometimes suffer unjustly | Though innocent, Christ was judged by Pilate to teach us to endure unjust treatment with patience
basis_note: Pilate declares Jesus not guilty yet sentences Him to the crowd's demand (Luke 23:14, 24). Christ redeemed us from the law's curse by becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:13), which supplies the freeing from judgment.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Does it have a special meaning that Christ was crucified and did not die in a different way?
answer: Yes. Thereby I am assured that He took upon Himself the curse which lay on me, for a crucified one was cursed by God.
right_choice: Yes. Thereby I am assured that He took upon Himself the curse which lay on me
wrong_choices: Yes. Thereby I am assured that Rome, not God, judged Him, so His cross carried no curse at all | No. Any other death would have won my pardon equally, since the manner of His dying made no difference | Yes. Thereby I am assured that He was the first martyr, whose example I must follow to be saved
basis_note: Galatians 3:13 says Christ became a curse for us, and Deuteronomy 21:23 says anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse. Together they teach that the cursed death Christ bore was hanging on a tree.
audit_why: The wrong choices were all roughly true (shameful, for criminals, what our sins deserved), so I replaced them with choices that clearly contradict the catechism's teaching that Christ bore the curse of God for us.

question: Why was it necessary for Christ to humble Himself even unto death?
answer: Because of the justice and truth of God satisfaction for our sins could be made in no other way than by the death of the Son of God.
right_choice: Because God's justice and truth required that satisfaction for our sins be made only through death of God's Son
wrong_choices: Because Satan held a lawful claim over sinners, and God's justice required that Christ's death be paid to him | Because our own good works and repentance, joined to Christ's example, could satisfy God's justice for our sins | Because God's mercy allowed our sins to be forgiven without any satisfaction, and Christ died only to set us an example
basis_note: Romans 3:25-26 shows God setting forth Christ's blood as the atoning sacrifice to demonstrate His righteousness and be just; Romans 8:3 says the law was powerless, so God sent His Son as an offering for sin.
audit_why: The three wrong choices all stated true teaching close to the catechism's answer, so I replaced them with choices that the catechism and the Bible clearly reject.

question: Why was he buried?
answer: His burial testified that He had really died.
right_choice: His burial testified that He had really died.
wrong_choices: To show that He was a criminal who deserved death | So His disciples would have a tomb to visit after | So that He would rise from the dead on the third day
basis_note: Scripture does not state the purpose of the burial, but the accounts show Jesus' body placed in a tomb after death, and Paul lists "that He was buried" between His death and resurrection, so the answer follows from them.
audit_why: One wrong choice (fulfilling prophecy) is also true, since Isaiah 53:9 foretold His burial, so it was replaced with a choice that is clearly wrong.

question: Since Christ has died for us, why do we still have to die?
answer: Our death is not a payment for our sins, but it puts an end to sin and is an entrance into eternal life.
right_choice: Our death is not payment for our sins but ends sin and enters eternal life
wrong_choices: Our death is payment for the sins that Christ's death did not cover | Our death is a punishment that makes us worthy of eternal life | Our death is a cleansing of guilt that must happen before we enter heaven
basis_note: Romans 6:7 says the one who has died is freed from sin, Philippians 1:23 speaks of departing to be with Christ, and 1 Thessalonians 5:10 says we will live with Him. Together they teach the answer's second half.
doubt: The shown verses do not say outright that our death is not a payment for sins; Romans 6:23 calls death the wages of sin, so that clause rests on the wider teaching that Christ alone paid.
audit_why: The three wrong choices were all true and close to the catechism's answer, so I replaced them with ideas the catechism and Scripture deny (death as payment, as merit, or as purifying). Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and wrong choices are sound, but the reference should point to Romans 6:7, Philippians 1:21-23, and 1 Thessalonians 5:10, which together directly support the Heidelberg Catechism's answer, rather than including John 5:24 (which doesn't address this point) and omitting Romans 6:7.

question: What further benefit do we receive from Christ's sacrifice and death on the cross?
answer: Through Christ's death our old nature is crucified, put to death, and buried with Him, so that the evil desires of the flesh may no longer reign in us, but that we may offer ourselves to Him as a sacrifice of thankfulness.
right_choice: Through Christ's death our old nature is crucified with Him so we may offer ourselves as a sacrifice to Him
wrong_choices: Through Christ's death we gain power to overcome temptation and to live in righteousness always | Through Christ's death we are freed from all evil desires so we naturally love holiness | Through Christ's death our guilt is removed so we no longer need to struggle against sin
basis_note: Romans 6:4 says we were buried with Christ, and Romans 6:6 says our old self was crucified with Him so sin's body is powerless. Romans 6:12 forbids sin to reign, and Romans 12:1 calls us to offer our bodies as living sacrifices.
audit_why: One wrong choice (sinful flesh put to death, living for God's glory) was nearly the same as the catechism's answer, so I replaced it with a choice that wrongly says we no longer need to struggle against sin.

question: Why is there added: He descended into hell?
answer: In my greatest sorrows and temptations I may be assured and comforted that my Lord Jesus Christ, by His unspeakable anguish, pain, terror, and agony, which He endured throughout all His sufferings but especially on the cross, has delivered me from the anguish and torment of hell.
right_choice: So that through His unspeakable suffering and agony, especially on the cross, Christ delivered us from hell's torment
wrong_choices: That Christ preached to the lost in hell after His death to give them a second chance to repent | That Christ went to the place of the dead to free the righteous souls held captive there | That Christ warned us to fear hell so that we would live holy lives out of terror
basis_note: Isaiah 53 says the punishment that brought us peace fell on the Servant and that He suffered anguish of soul; Matthew 27:46 records His cry of abandonment on the cross. The answer follows from these.
audit_why: Two wrong choices described Christ bearing hell's torment or separation from God, which is nearly what the catechism teaches, so they were replaced with choices that clearly contradict it.

question: How does Christ's resurrection benefit us?
answer: First, by His resurrection He has overcome death, so that He could make us share in the righteousness which He had obtained for us by His death. Second, by His power we too are raised up to a new life. Third, Christ's resurrection is to us a sure pledge of our glorious resurrection.
right_choice: By His resurrection Christ overcame death, shares righteousness with us, raises us to new life, and pledges our glorious resurrection
wrong_choices: By His resurrection Christ replaced the need for faith, removed all temptation from believers, and guarantees an earthly kingdom now | By His resurrection Christ ended all earthly suffering for believers, made us righteous by our own works, and promises worldly prosperity | By His resurrection Christ merely proved His divinity, gave us an example to follow, and promises that only our souls will live on
basis_note: Romans 4:25 ties Christ's resurrection to our justification, Ephesians 2:5-6 says God made us alive and raised us up with Christ, and 1 Corinthians 6:14 promises that God will raise us by His power.
audit_why: The catechism's answer is sound, but the wrong choices were true statements or nearly the same as the right one, so I replaced them with choices that clearly contradict the three benefits the catechism gives.

question: What do you confess when you say, He ascended into heaven?
answer: That Christ, before the eyes of His disciples, was taken up from the earth into heaven, and that He is there for our benefit until He comes again to judge the living and the dead.
right_choice: That Christ was taken up into heaven before His disciples and is there for our benefit until He comes to judge
wrong_choices: That Christ was taken up into heaven before His disciples and will never come back to earth again | That Christ was taken up into heaven before His disciples and there offers Himself again and again for us | That Christ was taken up into heaven in secret, unseen by His disciples, and is there for our benefit
basis_note: Acts 1:9 says the disciples watched as Jesus was taken up. Acts 1:11 promises His return. Heb 9:24 and Rom 8:34 say He now appears for us before God. The judgment of the living and dead is not stated in these verses.
audit_why: Three of the wrong choices were also true or nearly the same as the right answer (Christ interceding, preparing a place, awaiting judgment), so I replaced them with choices that contradict the Bible (Heb 9:25; Acts 1:9-11).

question: Is Christ, then, not with us until the end of the world, as He has promised us?
answer: Christ is true man and true God. With respect to His human nature He is no longer on earth, but with respect to His divinity, majesty, grace, and Spirit He is never absent from us.
right_choice: By His divinity, majesty, grace, and Spirit Christ is never absent from us; by His human nature He is no longer on earth.
wrong_choices: Christ is present on earth in His body in the bread and wine, though His divinity is only in heaven | Christ is no longer with us in any way, since He ascended to heaven and left the world behind | By His human nature Christ is still on earth everywhere, but by His divinity He is absent from us
basis_note: Jesus says He will no longer be in the world, going to the Father, yet promises to be with His people always. Colossians 2:9 says the full Deity dwells in Him in bodily form.
audit_why: The three wrong choices all repeated the catechism's own teaching, so they were also right; I replaced them with choices that contradict it and tightened the right choice to say His human nature is "no longer on earth."

question: But are the two natures in Christ not separated from each other if His human nature is not present wherever His divinity is?
answer: Not at all, for His divinity has no limits and is present everywhere. So it must follow that His divinity is indeed beyond the human nature which He has taken on and nevertheless is within this human nature and remains personally united with it.
right_choice: His divinity has no limits, is present everywhere, and is personally united with His human nature.
wrong_choices: His divinity and humanity are completely separate natures not truly united in one person. | His human nature became unlimited and present everywhere after His ascension to heaven. | His divine nature alone is truly present everywhere; His human nature exists nowhere.
basis_note: Jeremiah 23:23-24 teaches that the LORD fills heaven and earth and is not only nearby. Colossians 2:9 says the fullness of Deity dwells in Christ in bodily form, which supports the union of divinity with the human nature.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: How does Christ's ascension into heaven benefit us?
answer: First, He is our Advocate in heaven before His Father. Second, we have our flesh in heaven as a sure pledge that He, our Head, will also take us, His members, up to Himself. Third, He sends us His Spirit as a counter-pledge, by whose power we seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God, and not the things that are on earth.
right_choice: Our Advocate in heaven; our flesh there pledges He will take us; Spirit sent enables us to seek heavenly things.
wrong_choices: Our King ruling the earth now; our souls there are kept while bodies perish; Spirit sent makes us seek earthly blessings. | Our Priest offering sacrifice daily; our good works there earn our reward; Spirit sent frees us from all earthly troubles. | Our Teacher in heaven; our prayers there reach Him through the saints; Spirit sent lets us rest from seeking things above.
basis_note: Christ is our advocate before the Father (1 John 2:1), prepares a place for us and will receive us to Himself (John 14:2-3), and the Spirit is given as a pledge (2 Cor 5:5), so we seek things above (Col 3:1-2).
audit_why: The three wrong choices just repeated the catechism's three benefits in other words, so they were also right; they now state things the catechism and Bible do not teach, and the reference is tidied.

question: Why is it added, And sits at the right hand of God?
answer: Christ ascended into heaven to manifest Himself there as Head of His Church, through whom the Father governs all things.
right_choice: Christ ascended to manifest Himself as Head of His Church, through whom the Father governs all things.
wrong_choices: Christ ascended to leave His human nature behind so that only His divine nature remained in heaven | Christ ascended to rest from His work and hand the governing of all things over to the Church | Christ ascended to be separated from the earth and to await His return as judge of all
basis_note: Christ is seated at God's right hand and God made Him head over everything for the church, His body. Sitting there shows Him as exalted Head of the Church and ruler of all.
audit_why: Two wrong choices said Christ reigns in glory over all creation, which the Bible also teaches, so they were replaced with choices that clearly contradict the catechism's answer.

question: How does the glory of Christ, our Head, benefit us?
answer: First, by His Holy Spirit He pours out heavenly gifts upon us, His members. Second, by His power He defends and preserves us against all enemies.
right_choice: By His Spirit He pours out heavenly gifts; by His power He defends us against all enemies.
wrong_choices: By His example He shows us how to live; by His wisdom He helps us earn a place in heaven | By His Spirit He makes us perfectly holy now; by His power He frees us from all suffering in this life | By His blood He pays for our sins; by His power He gives us worldly wealth and success
basis_note: Acts 2:33 says the exalted Christ poured out the promised Holy Spirit; Psalm 110:1-2 has the Lord making His enemies a footstool and ruling in the midst of them, which supports His power defending His people.
audit_why: The right answer matches the Heidelberg Catechism, but the old wrong choices were also true or nearly the same (sanctifying us, guarding His church), so I replaced them with choices that clearly differ from the catechism's teaching.

question: What comfort is it to you that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead?
answer: In all my sorrow and persecution I lift up my head and eagerly await as judge from heaven the very same person who before has submitted Himself to the judgment of God for my sake, and has removed all the curse from me. He will cast all His and my enemies into everlasting condemnation, but He will take me and all His chosen ones to Himself into heavenly joy and glory.
right_choice: Christ, who bore God's judgment for me, will judge my enemies and bring me to glory.
wrong_choices: Christ will return to judge all humanity impartially and assign eternal rewards or punishments accordingly | Christ will examine all people's deeds and determine who deserves heaven based on their moral goodness | Christ will judge all people fairly based on their works, rewarding the good and punishing the evil
basis_note: Christ, revealed from heaven, repays affliction to those who afflict His people and gives relief to the oppressed; Matthew 25 shows Him separating the cursed from the righteous, who enter eternal life.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What do you believe concerning the Holy Spirit?
answer: First, He is, together with the Father and the Son, true and eternal God. Second, He is also given to me, to make me by true faith share in Christ and all His benefits, to comfort me, and to remain with me forever.
right_choice: He is true eternal God with Father and Son; given to share Christ with me, comfort me, and remain forever.
