wrong_choices: He is the highest of God's creatures; given to teach us, comfort us, and stay with us for a time | He is God's power at work in the world; given to make us holy and to guide our decisions | He is true God; given to enable our faith in Christ, to strengthen us, and to remain in our hearts
basis_note: Acts 5:3-4 equates lying to the Holy Spirit with lying to God, showing He is God. John 14:16-17 promises another Advocate to be with us forever, and Galatians 3:14 says we receive the Spirit by faith.
audit_why: The catechism answer is right, but one wrong choice was nearly the same as it, so it was replaced with a clearly wrong one (the Spirit as a created being who stays only for a time), and the reference was put in standard form.

question: What do you believe concerning the holy catholic Christian church?
answer: I believe that the Son of God, out of the whole human race, from the beginning of the world to its end, gathers, defends, and preserves for Himself, by His Spirit and Word, in the unity of the true faith, a church chosen to everlasting life. And I believe that I am and forever shall remain a living member of it.
right_choice: Christ gathers the church from all time through His Spirit and Word in true faith, and I'm a living member.
wrong_choices: The church is the people whom Christ calls to worship together and to serve Him through loving others | Christ founded the church to teach the ways of salvation and to bring all people into His kingdom | Christ established the church as His body with a visible structure and leadership for all the faithful to follow
basis_note: Christ says He will build His church against which the gates of Hades will not prevail, and no one can snatch His sheep from His hand. Revelation 5:9 says He purchased people from every nation, and Ephesians 1:4-5 says He chose us. Ephesians 4:13 and 5:26 add unity of faith and cleansing by the word.
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The catechism answer and its wrong choices are sound and none of the wrong choices is also right by the six verses that hold the answer, but the reference list was far too long and included verses for other catechism answers, so it has been trimmed to the six verses that actually hold this answer.

question: What do you understand by the communion of saints?
answer: First, that believers, all and everyone, as members of Christ have communion with Him and share in all His treasures and gifts. Second, that everyone is duty-bound to use his gifts readily and cheerfully for the benefit and well-being of the other members.
right_choice: Believers as Christ's members share in His treasures and gifts; everyone must use their gifts for others' benefit.
wrong_choices: Believers who have died as saints intercede for the living; everyone must pray to them for help | Only the most holy believers share in Christ's treasures; the rest must earn a share by their own good works | All Christians share the same spiritual gifts and blessings through their union with Christ in the church
basis_note: Believers are members of one body in Christ and share fellowship with the Father and Son (1 Cor 12:12-13; 1 John 1:3), and each should use his gift to serve one another (1 Pet 4:10).
audit_why: Two wrong choices were so close to the catechism's answer that they could fairly be picked, so they were replaced with choices that clearly contradict it and the Bible (1 Cor 12:4-13; Rom 12:4-8).

question: What do you believe concerning the forgiveness of sins?
answer: I believe that God, because of Christ's satisfaction, will no more remember my sins, nor my sinful nature, against which I have to struggle all my life, but He will graciously grant me the righteousness of Christ, that I may never come into condemnation.
right_choice: God won't remember my sins or sinful nature against me but grants me Christ's righteousness so I never face condemnation.
wrong_choices: God forgives my past sins through Christ, but I must earn forgiveness for my later sins by my own good works | God forgives my sins but still holds my sinful nature against me until I have overcome it by my own effort | God covers my sins with Christ's blood and then enables me to become righteous through faithful obedience
basis_note: God says He will remember sins no more (Heb 10:17), makes us the righteousness of God in Christ (2 Cor 5:21), and there is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1). The sinful nature is not named as forgiven, so that part is drawn from the proof texts.
audit_why: The catechism answer is sound, but two wrong choices described the Spirit's work of making us holy, which is also true, so they now describe earning forgiveness or righteousness by our own effort, which the catechism denies. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer, right choice, and wrong choices all hold up well against Hebrews 10:17, 2 Corinthians 5:21, and Romans 8:1, but Hebrews 10:17 (which directly supports 'will no more remember my sins') was missing from the reference list, so it has been added.

question: What comfort does the resurrection of the body offer you?
answer: Not only shall my soul after this life immediately be taken up to Christ, my Head, but also this my flesh, raised by the power of Christ, shall be reunited with my soul and made like Christ's glorious body.
right_choice: Soul goes to Christ; flesh is raised by His power, reunited with soul, made like His glorious body.
wrong_choices: My soul goes to heaven but my body remains sleeping in the earth eternally. | I will exist forever as a spirit in heaven completely without any body. | My body is raised purely spiritual and invisible, with no physical substance whatsoever.
basis_note: Luke 23:43 says the believer goes to be with Christ that same day, and Philippians 3:21 says Christ will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body. The reunion of flesh and soul is drawn from these.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What comfort do you receive from the article about the life everlasting?
answer: Since I now already feel in my heart the beginning of eternal joy, I shall after this life possess perfect blessedness, such as no eye has seen, no ear has heard, no heart has imagined—a blessedness in which to praise God forever.
right_choice: I already feel eternal joy's beginning in my heart; I will possess perfect blessedness beyond perception and praise God forever.
wrong_choices: I will someday reach perfect peace and joy when I depart from this world and enter God's presence | I feel no joy yet in this life; I will earn perfect blessedness after death by my own good works | I will later enjoy perfect peace and happiness forever in the presence of God in the heavenly place
basis_note: 1 Corinthians 2:9 gives the unseen, unheard, unimagined blessing God has prepared, Romans 14:17 names present joy in the Holy Spirit, and John 17:24 promises believers will be with Christ to see His glory.
audit_why: One wrong choice said almost what the catechism teaches (joy now, perfect blessedness later), so it was replaced with a choice that clearly contradicts it. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The Scripture quotation used KJV wording ("nor ear heard, nor the heart of man conceived") instead of the BSB's "no ear has heard, no heart has imagined," and the reference listed two verses (John 17:3; 2 Cor 5:2-3) that do not actually hold this answer, so both were corrected.

question: But what does it help you now that you believe all this?
answer: In Christ I am righteous before God and heir to life everlasting.
right_choice: In Christ I am righteous before God and heir to life everlasting.
wrong_choices: Through my faith in Christ I have earned my eternal life. | In Christ I am perfect in all my works and truly holy. | In Christ I am partially righteous and must hope for more righteousness.
basis_note: Romans 5:1 says believers are justified through faith and have peace with God through Christ; John 3:36 says whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. "Heir" is implied, not stated.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: How are you righteous before God?
answer: Only by true faith in Jesus Christ. Although my conscience accuses me that I have grievously sinned against all God's commandments, have never kept any of them, and am still inclined to all evil, yet God, without any merit of my own, out of mere grace, imputes to me the perfect satisfaction, righteousness, and holiness of Christ. He grants these to me as if I had never had nor committed any sin, and as if I myself had accomplished all the obedience which Christ has rendered for me, if only I accept this gift with a believing heart.
right_choice: Only by faith in Christ; God imputes Christ's satisfaction and righteousness to me as though I never sinned.
wrong_choices: By the work of the Holy Spirit making me righteous as I grow in holiness and obey God | By my genuine faith in Christ and by becoming increasingly righteous through moral effort and sincere obedience | By faith in Christ combined with my good works that show my sincere commitment to living a holy life
basis_note: Righteousness comes through faith in Jesus Christ, not works of the law (Rom 3:22; Gal 2:16), and in Christ we become the righteousness of God (2 Cor 5:21). The fuller imputation wording is drawn from these and the other proof texts.
audit_why: The question and answer match the catechism and the Bible (Romans 3:21-28; 4:3-5), and the wrong choices are clearly wrong by that teaching; only the short right choice was too long, so it was trimmed.

question: Why do you say that you are righteous only by faith?
answer: Not that I am acceptable to God on account of the worthiness of my faith, for only the satisfaction, righteousness, and holiness of Christ is my righteousness before God. I can receive this righteousness and make it mine in no other way than by faith only.
right_choice: Not because faith itself is righteous, but Christ's satisfaction and righteousness are mine; I receive them by faith only.
wrong_choices: Because the worthiness of my faith makes me acceptable to God | Because my faith and my obedience together complete the righteousness Christ began | Because faith is a good work that earns God's favor alongside Christ's merits
basis_note: Paul rejects his own righteousness and receives the righteousness from God through faith in Christ, and Christ himself is our righteousness (1 Cor 1:30). The answer's "faith only" is drawn from this contrast.
audit_why: The answer had a typo and strayed from the catechism's wording, and two wrong choices were really true statements about faith, so I restored the catechism's wording and replaced them with choices that make faith itself the ground of righteousness.

question: But why can our good works not be our righteousness before God, or at least a part of it?
answer: Because the righteousness which can stand before God's judgment must be absolutely perfect and in complete agreement with the law of God, whereas even our best works in this life are all imperfect and defiled with sin.
right_choice: God's law requires perfect righteousness; our best works are imperfect and defiled.
wrong_choices: God's law applies only to the Old Testament and no longer binds us. | God forbids good works and wants us to rest from all labor. | Our works are imperfect but still count toward at least half of righteousness.
basis_note: Galatians 3:10 requires continuing to do everything written in the law, so perfect obedience is needed, while Isaiah 64:6 says even our righteous acts are like filthy rags, showing our works are defiled.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: But do our good works earn nothing, even though God promises to reward them in this life and the next?
answer: This reward is not earned; it is a gift of grace.
right_choice: This reward is not earned; it is a gift of grace.
wrong_choices: God rewards the godly for their works out of obligation to them. | The reward for good works comes through our own merit and labor. | God only rewards those who perfectly obey all of His commands.
basis_note: Romans 11:6 says that if something is by grace it is no longer by works, so grace excludes earning. Luke 17:10 says faithful servants have only done their duty, so their service earns no reward.
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and wrong choices are sound, but the reference needed Romans 11:6 (which directly grounds the 'grace, not works' answer) alongside Luke 17:10, so it was updated to the verses that actually hold the answer.

question: Does this teaching not make people careless and wicked?
answer: No. It is impossible that those grafted into Christ by true faith should not bring forth fruits of thankfulness.
right_choice: No. It is impossible that those grafted into Christ by true faith should not bring forth fruits of thankfulness.
wrong_choices: Yes, many believers become careless about morality since they are assured that Christ paid for their sins | No, because good works must be done to earn God's favor, and that keeps people from becoming careless | No, but sincere believers must strive hard to produce good works to ensure they remain grafted into Christ
basis_note: John 15:5 says those who remain in Christ bear much fruit, and Matthew 7:18 says a good tree cannot bear bad fruit, so union with Christ yields fruit.
audit_why: One wrong choice (that believers may struggle to bear fruit) is true enough that it could also be chosen, so it was replaced with a choice that clearly contradicts salvation by grace.

question: Since then faith alone makes us share in Christ and all His benefits, where does this faith come from?
answer: From the Holy Spirit, who works it in our hearts by the preaching of the gospel, and strengthens it by the use of the sacraments.
right_choice: From the Holy Spirit, who works it by the gospel and strengthens it through the sacraments.
wrong_choices: From God's free choice and from our own personal decision to believe in Christ as our Savior | From our own good works and from the church's rituals that earn us a share in Christ's benefits | From our parents' faith and from Christian education that teaches us to believe in Jesus as our Lord
basis_note: Faith comes by hearing the word of Christ (Rom 10:17), is the gift of God (Eph 2:8), and is born of the Spirit (John 3:5). The verses shown do not speak of sacraments strengthening faith.
audit_why: One wrong choice (the Word of God and the Holy Spirit working through reason) was nearly the same as the catechism's answer, so it was replaced with a clearly wrong choice about earning faith by works and rituals.

question: What are the sacraments?
answer: The sacraments are holy, visible signs and seals. They were instituted by God so that by their use He might the more fully declare and seal to us the promise of the gospel. And this is the promise: that God graciously grants us forgiveness of sins and everlasting life because of the one sacrifice of Christ accomplished on the cross.
right_choice: Holy visible signs and seals instituted by God declaring and sealing forgiveness and eternal life through Christ's one sacrifice.
wrong_choices: Holy means of grace established by Christ that mysteriously convey God's forgiveness and spiritual power to the faithful | Sacred ceremonies and rituals instituted by the church that remind us of Christ's work and Christian commitment | Outward religious ceremonies that symbolize our faith in Christ and demonstrate our dedication to the Christian life
basis_note: Romans 4:11 calls circumcision a sign and seal, Genesis 17:11 a sign of the covenant instituted by God, and Matthew 26:28 and Hebrews 10:10 tie the signs to forgiveness through Christ's once-for-all sacrifice.
audit_why: The answer matches the Heidelberg Catechism, but the reference "Rom 4:1" should be Rom 4:11, where circumcision is called a sign and seal, so the reference was corrected. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The catechism answer and wrong choices check out against the four verses given (circumcision as sign/seal of righteousness by faith in Rom 4:11 and Gen 17:11, the blood of the covenant for forgiveness in Matt 26:28, and the once-for-all sacrifice in Heb 10:10); only the reference list was trimmed to match exactly the verses confirmed to hold the answer, dropping Deut 30:6 and Acts 2:38 which were not part of this check.

question: According to the Heidelberg Catechism, what does the Holy Spirit teach us in the gospel and assure us by the sacraments that our entire salvation rests on?
answer: Christ's one sacrifice for us on the cross. The Holy Spirit teaches this in the gospel and assures us of it by the sacraments.
right_choice: Christ's one sacrifice for us on the cross
wrong_choices: Our own obedience to God's law and good works | The church's repeated offering of Christ in the sacraments | Our growth in holiness through the Lord's Supper
basis_note: Hebrews 10:10 names the one sacrifice of Christ's body once for all; Romans 6:3 and 1 Corinthians 11:26 tie baptism and the Lord's Supper to His death; Ephesians 1:13 links hearing the gospel with being sealed by the Spirit.
audit_why: The original wrong choices were also true (the Word and sacraments do point us to Christ), so the question now asks what our salvation rests on, with clearly wrong choices. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The question, answer, and wrong choices are all sound, but the reference should point to the verses the catechism actually uses (Heb 10:10; Rom 6:3; 1 Cor 11:26; Eph 1:13) rather than Gal 3:27, which was swapped in.

question: How many sacraments has Christ instituted in the new covenant?
answer: Two: holy baptism and the holy supper.
right_choice: Two: holy baptism and the holy supper.
wrong_choices: Seven: baptism, confirmation, penance, eucharist, unction, orders, and matrimony. | Three: baptism, the supper, and confirmation as practiced in the church. | One: only baptism, as the supper is merely a memorial meal.
basis_note: Christ commands baptism in Matthew 28:19 and institutes the Lord's Supper in 1 Corinthians 11:24-25. The count of two follows from these two institutions, though the verses do not use the word "sacrament" or state the number.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: How does holy baptism signify and seal to you that the one sacrifice of Christ on the cross benefits you?
answer: In this way: Christ instituted this outward washing and with it gave the promise that, as surely as water washes away the dirt from the body, so certainly His blood and Spirit wash away the impurity of my soul, that is, all my sins.
right_choice: Water in baptism washes dirt as His blood and Spirit wash away all my sins, Christ's promise at His institution.
wrong_choices: Just as water cleanses the body completely, so the sacrament of baptism miraculously removes all our sins | Baptism is an outward sign that we have already been cleansed inwardly and commit ourselves to Christ | Water cleanses dirt from the body, and baptism through God's sacramental action miraculously cleanses our soul
basis_note: Acts 2:38 links baptism with forgiveness of sins and the Spirit; Hebrews 9:14 says Christ's blood purifies the conscience; Hebrews 10:22 pairs washing with pure water with cleansing from a guilty conscience.
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The reference did not include Hebrews 9:14 and Hebrews 10:22, which together with Acts 2:38 actually hold the catechism's answer about Christ's blood and Spirit washing away sin, so the reference was corrected to include them.

question: What does it mean to be washed with Christ's blood and Spirit?
answer: To be washed with Christ's blood means to receive forgiveness of sins from God, through grace, because of Christ's blood, poured out for us in His sacrifice on the cross. To be washed with His Spirit means to be renewed by the Holy Spirit and sanctified to be members of Christ, so that more and more we become dead to sin and lead a holy and blameless life.
right_choice: Christ's blood washes away sins through grace; His Spirit renews and sanctifies us to live holy.
wrong_choices: Washed with blood means we never sin again; washed with Spirit means perfect knowledge. | Blood means outward cleansing; Spirit means inner peace and emotional comfort only. | Blood washes priests; Spirit washes believers; together they make us completely sinless.
basis_note: Ephesians 1:7 gives forgiveness of trespasses through Christ's blood and God's grace. Ezekiel 36:26, 1 Corinthians 6:11 and Romans 6:4 show the Spirit renewing and sanctifying believers and bringing newness of life.
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and wrong choices hold up under Ephesians 1:7, Ezekiel 36:26, 1 Corinthians 6:11, and Romans 6:4, but Ezekiel 36:26 (the 'new heart and new spirit' verse that backs the Spirit-renewal part of the answer) was missing from the reference list, so it was added alongside the verse already there.

question: Where has Christ promised that He will wash us with His blood and Spirit as surely as we are washed with the water of baptism?
answer: In the institution of baptism, where He says: “Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” and “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.” This promise is repeated where Scripture speaks of baptism as the washing of new birth and the washing away of sins.
right_choice: In the institution of baptism, a promise repeated where Scripture speaks of the washing of new birth
wrong_choices: In the story of His own baptism, where the Spirit descended on Him like a dove | In the Sermon on the Mount, where He promises that the pure in heart will see God | In the institution of the Lord’s Supper, where He tells us to eat the bread and drink the cup
basis_note: The answer points to Christ's baptismal commission and to passages calling baptism a washing: Titus 3:5 speaks of the washing of new birth and renewal by the Spirit, and Acts 22:16 of washing sins away.
audit_why: The answer used non-BSB wording (such as "He who believes" and "washing of regeneration"), and the wrong choices were all nearly the same as the right one, so the answer now quotes the BSB and the wrong choices name other places in Scripture.

question: Does this outward washing with water itself wash away sins?
answer: No, only the blood of Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit cleanse us from all sins.
right_choice: No, only the blood of Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit cleanse us from all sins.
wrong_choices: Yes, but only if the person being baptized has perfect faith and repentance. | Yes, water washes sins away, while the Spirit provides additional grace and comfort. | Yes, water itself has cleansing power when used in baptism by a priest.
basis_note: 1 John 1:7 says the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin; 1 Corinthians 6:11 says believers were washed by the Spirit; 1 Peter 3:21 says baptism is not the removal of dirt from the body.
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and wrong choices are sound, but the reference cited Matt 3:11, which does not actually hold this answer; it should instead cite 1 John 1:7, 1 Peter 3:21, and 1 Corinthians 6:11, the verses that teach the blood of Christ and the Spirit (not water) cleanse from sin.

question: Why does the Holy Spirit call baptism the washing of new birth and renewal, and the washing away of sins?
answer: God speaks in this way for a good reason. He wants to teach us that the blood and Spirit of Christ remove our sins just as water takes away dirt from the body. But, even more important, He wants to assure us by this divine pledge and sign that we are as truly cleansed from our sins spiritually as we are bodily washed with water.
right_choice: God teaches blood and Spirit remove sins like water removes dirt, and assures us we're truly cleansed spiritually as bodily.
wrong_choices: The Holy Spirit teaches that baptism is a powerful means through which God actually cleanses us from sin | God declares that through baptism the water magically transforms us so that all our sins are completely erased | God wants us to know that baptism physically removes the stains of sin just as water removes dirt
reference: 1 Cor 6:11; Titus 3:5; Rev 1:5; Rev 7:14; Mark 16:16; Acts 2:38; Rom 6:3-4; Gal 3:27; Acts 22:16; 1 Peter 3:21
basis_note: Titus 3:5 calls baptism the washing of new birth and renewal by the Spirit, Acts 22:16 says baptism washes sins away, and 1 Peter 3:21 calls the water a pledge of a clear conscience.
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The question's wording ('washing of regeneration') followed the KJV instead of the BSB's 'washing of new birth and renewal'; it was reworded to match the BSB text while the answer and choices, which already fit Titus 3:5, Acts 22:16 and 1 Peter 3:21, were kept unchanged.

question: Should infants, too, be baptized?
answer: Yes. Infants as well as adults belong to God's covenant and congregation. Through Christ's blood the redemption from sin and the Holy Spirit, who works faith, are promised to them no less than to adults. Therefore, by baptism, as sign of the covenant, they must be grafted into the Christian church and distinguished from the children of unbelievers. This was done in the old covenant by circumcision, in place of which baptism was instituted in the new covenant.
right_choice: Yes, infants belong to God's covenant and receive redemption and Spirit; baptism grafts them into the church replacing circumcision.
wrong_choices: Yes, because baptism itself washes away the sin they inherited from Adam and makes them children of God | Yes, infants must be baptized immediately so they can receive God's grace and be part of God's covenant | Yes, but only when both parents are church members, since the covenant promise belongs to them alone
basis_note: Acts 2:39 says the promise belongs to believers' children, Genesis 17:7 makes the covenant with descendants, and Colossians 2:11-12 links baptism with circumcision as the sign of the covenant.
audit_why: Two wrong choices were so close to the catechism's teaching (belonging to Christian parents, being marked as God's people) that they could be picked, so they were replaced with choices that clearly contradict it.

question: How does the Lord's Supper signify and seal to you that you share in Christ's one sacrifice on the cross and in all His gifts?
answer: In this way: Christ has commanded me and all believers to eat of this broken bread and drink of this cup in remembrance of Him. With this command He gave these promises: First, as surely as I see with my eyes the bread of the Lord broken for me and the cup given to me, so surely was His body offered for me and His blood poured out for me on the cross. Second, as surely as I receive from the hand of the minister and taste with my mouth the bread and the cup of the Lord as sure signs of Christ's body and blood, so surely does He Himself nourish and refresh my soul to everlasting life with His crucified body and shed blood.
right_choice: As surely as I receive bread and cup, so surely Christ was offered for me and nourishes my soul.
wrong_choices: Commands remembrance of His sacrifice through this sacred meal; the bread and wine are His actual flesh and blood present | As surely as I receive bread and cup, so surely the priest repeats Christ's sacrifice to earn my forgiveness | Christ commanded us to eat the bread and drink the cup to remember His death; these elements truly are His body and blood
basis_note: Christ commands eating and drinking in remembrance of Him, His body is given and broken for you, His blood poured out for you, and whoever eats His flesh and drinks His blood has eternal life.
audit_why: One wrong choice said Christ feeds our souls in the meal, which is just what the catechism teaches, so it was replaced with a wrong teaching (a repeated sacrifice), and the right choice was shortened and now includes the promise that Christ's body was offered for me. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and choices faithfully reflect the Heidelberg Catechism's teaching and the cited BSB passages, but the reference left out John 6:54, which underlies the promise of the Supper nourishing the soul to everlasting life, so the reference was corrected to the three verses that actually hold the answer.

question: What does it mean to eat the crucified body of Christ and to drink His shed blood?
answer: First, to accept with a believing heart all the suffering and the death of Christ, and so receive forgiveness of sins and life eternal. Second, to be united more and more to His sacred body through the Holy Spirit, who lives both in Christ and in us. Therefore, although Christ is in heaven and we are on earth, yet we are flesh of His flesh and bone of His bones, and we forever live and are governed by one Spirit, as the members of our body are by one soul.
right_choice: To accept Christ's suffering and death for forgiveness and be united with His body through the Spirit.
wrong_choices: To believe that Christ's literal body is present in the bread and wine through the priest's blessing. | To accept Christ's suffering by faith while remaining spiritually separate from His body until heaven. | To commemorate Christ's death through eating bread and wine as reminders and symbols only.
basis_note: John 6:35 equates coming to Christ and believing with never hungering or thirsting; John 6:56 says eating and drinking means remaining in Christ, and 1 John 4:13 ties that abiding to the Spirit.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Where has Christ promised that He will nourish and refresh believers with His body and blood as surely as they eat of this broken bread and drink of this cup?
answer: In the institution of the Lord's Supper: "The Lord Jesus, on the night He was betrayed, took bread, and when He had given thanks, He broke it and said, 'This is My body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of Me.' In the same way, after supper He took the cup, saying, 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me.' For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes." Paul repeats this promise: "Is not the cup of blessing that we bless a participation in the blood of Christ? And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf."
right_choice: At the institution of the Lord's Supper, and in Paul's words on sharing in Christ's body and blood.
wrong_choices: At Pentecost when the Holy Spirit was given to believers at the breaking of bread. | In the feeding of the five thousand where Christ multiplied loaves and fishes for the multitude. | At the Transfiguration where Christ was glorified with Moses and Elijah, eating and drinking with them.
basis_note: The answer is the institution of the Lord's Supper, where Christ says of the bread and cup, "This is My body" and "This cup is the new covenant in My blood," and 1 Corinthians 10:16-17 repeats it as participation in His body and blood.
audit_why: The Bible quotations in the answer now follow the BSB word for word (including "This cup is the new covenant in My blood" and "one loaf"), and the right choice is shortened so it fits the limit and no longer stands out.

question: Are then the bread and wine changed into the real body and blood of Christ?
answer: No. Just as the water of baptism is not changed into the blood of Christ and is not the washing away of sins itself but is simply God's sign and pledge, so also the bread in the Lord's supper does not become the body of Christ itself, although it is called Christ's body in keeping with the nature and usage of sacraments.
right_choice: No. Water isn't changed to blood in baptism; bread isn't changed to body in supper but is called so sacramentally.
wrong_choices: Yes. Through the priest's consecration the bread is transformed into the real body of Christ. | No. But the bread becomes Christ's body through God's power even though nothing appears to change. | Yes. Though it remains bread in appearance, the substance is miraculously changed into Christ's body.
basis_note: Scripture never states the bread is not changed. It is taught: Christ calls the bread His body (Matt 26:26), Paul calls it bread and a participation in the body (1 Cor 10:16), and Peter says the water symbolizes baptism (1 Pet 3:21).
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Why then does Christ call the bread His body and the cup His blood, or the new covenant in His blood, and why does Paul speak of a participation in the body and blood of Christ?
answer: Christ speaks in this way for a good reason: He wants to teach us by His supper that as bread and wine sustain us in this temporal life, so His crucified body and shed blood are true food and drink for our souls to eternal life. But, even more important, He wants to assure us by this visible sign and pledge, first, that through the working of the Holy Spirit we share in His true body and blood as surely as we receive with our mouth these holy signs in remembrance of Him, and, second, that all His suffering and obedience are as certainly ours as if we personally had suffered and paid for our sins.
right_choice: Bread nourishes bodies as His body nourishes souls eternally; by Spirit we truly share in Him and His suffering becomes ours.
wrong_choices: The bread and wine are merely symbols of Christ's body and blood with no real spiritual significance to believers | The bread and wine physically transform into His body and blood through the priest's consecration for literal consumption | Through priestly blessing, Christ's body is daily re-offered for the sins of both living and dead
basis_note: Scripture calls Christ's flesh real food and His blood real drink (John 6:55), speaks of sharing in His body and blood (1 Cor 10:16), and says we are united with Him in His death (Rom 6:5).
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What difference is there between the Lord's supper and the papal mass?
answer: The Lord's supper testifies to us, first, that we have complete forgiveness of all our sins through the one sacrifice of Jesus Christ, which He Himself accomplished on the cross once for all; and, second, that through the Holy Spirit we are grafted into Christ, who with His true body is now in heaven at the right hand of the Father, and this is where He wants to be worshipped. But the mass teaches, first, that the living and the dead do not have forgiveness of sins through the suffering of Christ unless He is still offered for them daily by the priests; and, second, that Christ is bodily present in the form of bread and wine, and there is to be worshipped. Therefore the mass is basically nothing but a denial of the one sacrifice and suffering of Jesus Christ, and an accursed idolatry.
right_choice: Supper witnesses complete forgiveness through Christ's one sacrifice; mass wrongly teaches daily re-offering and worship of Christ bodily present in bread.
wrong_choices: Both Supper and mass teach that Christ is present in the bread and wine to be worshipped by believers | The Lord's Supper teaches that forgiveness needs daily offering by priests, while the mass rests on Christ's one sacrifice on the cross | The Lord's Supper and the mass are essentially the same, both offering Christ's sacrifice daily for the living and dead
basis_note: Scripture teaches Christ offered one sacrifice for all time, so no further offering is needed, and that He sits at God's right hand in heaven, where He is worshipped in spirit and truth. The verses never mention the papal mass, so that description is the catechism's judgment.
audit_why: One wrong choice described what the mass teaches, which matches the catechism, so I replaced it with a reversed statement that is clearly wrong.

question: Who are to come to the table of the Lord?
answer: Those who are truly displeased with themselves because of their sins and yet trust that these are forgiven them and that their remaining weakness is covered by the suffering and death of Christ, and who also desire more and more to strengthen their faith and amend their life. But hypocrites and those who do not repent eat and drink judgment upon themselves.
right_choice: Those displeased with their sins who trust Christ's death covers them and want to strengthen faith and amend life.
wrong_choices: Only the spiritually mature and morally pure who have overcome their greatest temptations and weaknesses. | All baptized members of the Christian church who profess belief in Christ and are confirmed communicants. | Those who have confessed their sins to the minister and promise to endeavor to live better.
basis_note: Paul tells each person to examine himself before eating the bread and drinking the cup, and warns that whoever eats without recognizing the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.
audit_why: The catechism answer is right, but the reference now cites only 1 Corinthians 11:26-32, since 10:19-22 is about the table of demons, and the short right choice is trimmed to fit the length limit.

question: Are those also to be admitted to the Lord's Supper who by their confession and life show that they are unbelieving and ungodly?
answer: No, for then God's covenant would be profaned and His wrath kindled against the whole congregation. The church must exclude such persons by the keys of the kingdom of heaven until they amend their lives.
right_choice: No. The covenant would be profaned and God's wrath kindled. The church must exclude them by ecclesiastical discipline.
wrong_choices: Only if they refuse to repent; those showing some signs of faith should be permitted. | No, but the church should admit them secretly to avoid seeming harsh or judgmental toward them. | Yes. The supper should be offered to all as a means toward their eventual conversion.
basis_note: Paul tells the church not to associate with or even eat with a professing brother living in open sin, and to expel such a wicked man; Psalm 50:16 rebukes the wicked who recite God's covenant with their lips.
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and choices are sound, but the reference lacked 1 Corinthians 5:11,13, which directly supports the command to exclude unrepentant, ungodly persons ('do not even eat'; 'expel the wicked man from among you'), so it was added to the reference.

question: What are the keys of the kingdom of heaven?
answer: The preaching of the holy gospel and church discipline. By these two the kingdom of heaven is opened to believers and closed to unbelievers.
right_choice: Gospel preaching and church discipline. These open the kingdom to believers and close it to unbelievers.
wrong_choices: The authority of priests alone to forgive sins and administer the sacraments to cleanse the congregation | The apostle Peter alone, to whom Christ gave the exclusive keys to bind and loose all sins eternally | Prayer and fasting by the church leaders, by which the kingdom is spiritually opened to the worthy
basis_note: Matthew 16:19 gives the keys of the kingdom and binding and loosing. John 20:21-23 has Christ sending the disciples and giving authority to forgive or withhold forgiveness, which the answer draws out as preaching and church discipline.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: How is the kingdom of heaven opened and closed by the preaching of the gospel?
answer: According to the command of Christ, the kingdom of heaven is opened when it is proclaimed and publicly testified to each and every believer that God has really forgiven all their sins for the sake of Christ's merits, as often as they by true faith accept the promise of the gospel. The kingdom of heaven is closed when it is proclaimed and testified to all unbelievers and hypocrites that the wrath of God and eternal condemnation rest on them as long as they do not repent. According to this testimony of the gospel, God will judge both in this life and in the life to come.
right_choice: It opens by proclaiming God's forgiveness to believers and closes by proclaiming His wrath on unrepentant unbelievers.
wrong_choices: The gospel proclaims forgiveness to all people indiscriminately, promising that God's love prevents any from experiencing His eternal wrath | The gospel declares that believers receive automatic forgiveness without repentance, while unbelievers face eternal separation from God's presence | Gospel preaching by the church opens the kingdom only to those who receive the sacraments from authorized priests
basis_note: Christ sends the disciples and says forgiven sins are forgiven when they are forgiven (John 20:21-23). The wrath of God remains on whoever rejects the Son (John 3:36). Together they teach the answer's two sides.
audit_why: The catechism answer and the wrong choices are sound, but the short right choice was one word too long, so it was reworded more briefly with the same meaning.

question: How is the kingdom of heaven closed and opened by church discipline?
answer: According to the command of Christ, people who call themselves Christians but show themselves to be unchristian in doctrine or life are first repeatedly admonished in a brotherly manner. If they do not give up their errors or wickedness, they are reported to the church, that is, to the elders. If they do not heed also their admonitions, they are forbidden the use of the sacraments, and they are excluded by the elders from the Christian congregation, and by God Himself from the kingdom of Christ. They are again received as members of Christ and of the church when they promise and show real amendment.
right_choice: Unchristian members are admonished, reported to elders, forbidden sacraments, and excluded. They're received back when they show real amendment.
wrong_choices: Church discipline immediately excommunicates those who sin without any chance for repentance or restoration to the church community | Members showing unchristian behavior should be privately criticized by elders but allowed to continue receiving all church sacraments | Sinful church members are permanently barred from the church once admonished, never permitted to return regardless of their later repentance
basis_note: Matthew 18:15-18 gives the stages of brotherly admonition, reporting to the church, and binding and loosing; 1 Corinthians 5:11-13 gives non-association and expulsion; 2 Corinthians 2:6-8 gives restoration after repentance. "Elders" and "forbidden the sacraments" are inferred, not stated.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Since we have been delivered from our misery by grace alone through Christ, without any merit of our own, why must we yet do good works?
answer: Because Christ, having redeemed us by His blood, also renews us by His Holy Spirit to be His image, so that with our whole life we may show ourselves thankful to God for His benefits, and He may be praised by us. Further, that we ourselves may be assured of our faith by its fruits, and that by our godly walk of life we may win our neighbours for Christ.
right_choice: Show thankfulness to God and praise Him; assure ourselves of faith by its fruits; win neighbors to Christ by godly living.
wrong_choices: We do good works because Christ's redemption obligates us to keep God's law perfectly to maintain our salvation | Good works are necessary to earn God's favor, since our justification depends on the quality of our righteous deeds | Good works are optional displays of superior piety for Christians, but are not required by God for any believer
basis_note: Believers offer their bodies as living sacrifices and are transformed by renewed minds; their good deeds let others see and glorify God; practicing these things makes their calling sure.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Can those be saved who do not turn to God from their ungrateful and impenitent walk of life?
answer: By no means. Scripture says that no unchaste person, idolater, adulterer, thief, greedy person, drunkard, slanderer, robber, or the like shall inherit the kingdom of God.
right_choice: By no means. No unchaste person, idolater, adulterer, thief, greedy person, drunkard, slanderer, or robber shall inherit God's kingdom.
wrong_choices: Only those who refuse to turn are lost; those who once believed keep their salvation. | Yes. God's mercy and Christ's sacrifice forgive all sins regardless of the sinner's repentance. | Yes. If they have faith alone they will be saved despite their continued impenitent lifestyle.
basis_note: Paul says the wicked, including the sexually immoral, idolaters, adulterers, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, and verbal abusers, will not inherit the kingdom of God. Galatians 5:21 says the same of those who practice such things.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What is the true repentance or conversion of man?
answer: It is the dying of the old nature and the coming to life of the new.
right_choice: It is the dying of the old nature and the coming to life of the new.
wrong_choices: Repentance is confessing our sins to a priest and receiving his absolution. | Repentance is obeying God's law perfectly for the rest of our life on earth. | Repentance is making satisfaction and payment to God for our sinful acts.
basis_note: Colossians 3:5 says to put to death the components of the earthly nature, and 3:10 says to put on the new self being renewed. That matches dying of the old nature and new life.
audit_why: One wrong choice, sorrow for sin, is part of what the catechism calls the dying of the old nature, so it was replaced with a choice that is clearly wrong.

question: What is the dying of the old nature?
answer: It is to grieve with heartfelt sorrow that we have offended God by our sin, and more and more to hate it and flee from it.
right_choice: To grieve with heartfelt sorrow that we offended God by sin, and increasingly to hate and flee from it.
wrong_choices: To feel deep regret for the consequences of sin but without necessarily rejecting sin itself as offensive to God | To recognize that sinning is wrong in theory while continuing to practice sin with an understanding that grace covers it | To temporarily mourn one's sins while aware they will be forgiven, and then gradually to move beyond the grief
basis_note: David confesses that he has sinned against God, and 2 Corinthians 7:10 speaks of godly sorrow that leads to repentance. Romans 8:13 urges putting to death the deeds of the body.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What is the coming to life of the new nature?
answer: It is a heartfelt joy in God through Christ, and a love and delight to live according to the will of God in all good works.
right_choice: Heartfelt joy in God through Christ, and love and delight to live according to God's will in all good works.
wrong_choices: A temporary emotional high when experiencing God's blessings, which gradually fades as life's difficulties and challenges accumulate | The determination to obey God's law through human effort and willpower, demonstrating one's superior righteousness compared to others | The feeling of satisfaction that comes from successfully performing good works and receiving praise from Christian community members
basis_note: Psalm 51:12 asks for restored joy in God's salvation and a willing spirit; Romans 14:17 names joy in the Holy Spirit; Ephesians 2:10 says believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and wrong choices match the Heidelberg Catechism's teaching and the cited verses well; only the reference was trimmed to the three verses that actually hold the answer, instead of a long list of proof texts, some of which do not directly support the specific wording given.

question: But what are good works?
answer: Only those which are done out of true faith, in accordance with the law of God, and to His glory, and not those based on our own opinion or on precepts of men.
right_choice: Works from true faith, according to God's law, to His glory, not based on our opinions or human precepts.
wrong_choices: Works that comply with church traditions and the teachings of learned religious leaders, even if Scripture seems to suggest otherwise | Works that accomplish much good in society and receive approval from communities, regardless of the religious motives behind them | Works that feel morally right to our conscience, whether or not they align with specific biblical commands or principles
basis_note: Romans 14:23 says what is not from faith is sin; Leviticus 18:4 requires keeping God's judgments; 1 Corinthians 10:31 directs all to God's glory; Matthew 15:9 rejects worship taught as men's precepts.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What is the law of the LORD?
answer: And God spoke all these words: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. (1) You shall have no other gods before Me. (2) You shall not make for yourself an idol in the form of anything in the heavens above, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath. You shall not bow down to them or worship them; for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on their children to the third and fourth generations of those who hate Me, but showing loving devotion to a thousand generations of those who love Me and keep My commandments. (3) You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not leave anyone unpunished who takes His name in vain. (4) Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy. Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God, on which you must not do any work—neither you, nor your son or daughter, nor your manservant or maidservant or livestock, nor the foreigner within your gates. For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them, but on the seventh day He rested. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and set it apart as holy. (5) Honor your father and mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you. (6) You shall not murder. (7) You shall not commit adultery. (8) You shall not steal. (9) You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. (10) You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, or his manservant or maidservant, or his ox or donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.”
right_choice: The Ten Commandments of God revealed to Moses at Mount Sinai.
wrong_choices: The ceremonial laws of Moses regarding sacrifices, feasts, and temple worship. | The laws of Christ summed up in the twofold command to love. | The civil laws of Israel for governing their kingdom and their nation.
basis_note: The answer is the text of the Ten Commandments, which Exodus 20:1-17 gives as the words God spoke: "And God spoke all these words," followed by the commandments.
audit_why: The catechism's answer quoted the Ten Commandments in older wording (graven image, bondage, labour, ass) with stray repeated numbers, so it now gives the BSB text of Exodus 20 with each commandment numbered once.

question: How are these commandments divided?
answer: Into two parts. The first teaches us how to live in relation to God; the second, what duties we owe our neighbor.
right_choice: Into two parts: first, how to live toward God; second, our duties toward our neighbor.
wrong_choices: Into three parts: our duties to God, to ourselves, and to our neighbors. | Into two parts: external actions and internal thoughts and desires of the heart. | Into ten parts, one for each commandment, each with its own purpose and reason.
basis_note: Jesus sets the law in two parts: love the Lord your God first and greatest, and love your neighbor as yourself, with all the Law hanging on these two.
audit_why: The teaching is right and matches Jesus' two great commandments in Matthew 22, but the answer used the spelling "neighbour" while the BSB and the other choices use "neighbor", so I changed it to match.

question: What does the LORD require in the first commandment?
answer: That for the sake of my very salvation I avoid and flee all idolatry, witchcraft, superstition, and prayer to saints or to other creatures. Further, that I rightly come to know the only true God, trust in Him alone, submit to Him with all humility and patience, expect all good from Him only, and love, fear, and honor Him with all my heart. In short, that I forsake all creatures rather than do the least thing against His will.
right_choice: Flee idolatry, trust the only God alone, love and fear Him, and forsake all creatures rather than disobey Him.
wrong_choices: Believe that God exists, avoid speaking His name irreverently, and acknowledge Him publicly without necessarily obeying all His commands | Trust and obey the one God while maintaining loyalty to family, nation, and personal ambitions within reasonable limits always | Acknowledge that God is supreme while respecting other religions' worship practices and integrating their wisdom into your personal faith
basis_note: The answer is drawn from the proof texts: flee idolatry and witchcraft (Deut 18, 1 Cor 10:14), worship no creature (Rev 22:8-9), worship God alone (Matt 4:10), know, trust, and love Him (John 17:3, Jer 17:7, Deut 6:5), and expect good from Him (Jas 1:17).
audit_why: The catechism answer is right and the wrong choices are clearly wrong, but a period in the answer should be a comma, and the short right choice was too long, so it was tightened.

question: What is idolatry?
answer: Idolatry is having or inventing something in which to put our trust instead of, or in addition to, the only true God who has revealed Himself in His Word.
right_choice: Having or inventing something to trust in instead of or along with the only true God revealed in His Word.
wrong_choices: Refusing to worship any god because of doubt about God's existence or the reliability of Scripture's testimony about Him | Taking God's name in vain by swearing falsely or speaking carelessly when using His name | Desiring what belongs to our neighbor, such as his house, his possessions, or anything that is his
basis_note: Only the LORD made the heavens, while other gods are idols (1 Chr 16:26). Idols are trusted and made (Ps 31:6; Hab 2:18), and a god can be one's belly (Phil 3:19).
audit_why: Two wrong choices (making images for worship, and honoring other gods alongside God) are also forms of idolatry, and "graven idols" is KJV wording, so they were replaced with choices about other commandments. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The old reference (Gal 4:8-9; Eph 5:5) linked idolatry to greed/covetousness, which risked making the "coveting our neighbor's goods" wrong choice seem also correct; the reference is corrected to 1 Chr 16:26, Phil 3:19, Ps 31:6 and Hab 2:18, which plainly teach that idolatry is trusting in something other than, or besides, the true God, without that overlap.

question: What does God require in the second commandment?
answer: We are not to make an image of God in any way, nor to worship Him in any other manner than He has commanded in His Word.

question: May we then not make any image at all?
answer: No. God cannot and may not be visibly portrayed in any way. Creatures may be portrayed, but God forbids us to make or have any images of them in order to worship them or to serve God through them.
right_choice: No. God cannot be visibly portrayed. Creatures may be portrayed, but forbidden for worship or serving God through them.
wrong_choices: We may make images of creatures but are forbidden from making any images whatsoever, since all image-making displeases God | Images of any kind are prohibited absolutely, including images of creatures and saints, because all represent turning from God | Yes, we may make images of God for churches to help people understand divine nature and to aid in worship
basis_note: Israel saw no form of God at Horeb, so they must not make an idol in the form of man, beast, bird, creeping thing, or fish. The prohibition targets idols made to be worshipped.
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The teaching and wrong choices are sound Heidelberg Catechism content, but the reference failed to include Deut 4:15-17, the passage that actually supplies the key claim that God cannot be visibly portrayed; that reference has been added.

question: But may images not be tolerated in the churches as "books for the laity"?
answer: No, for we should not be wiser than God. He wants His people to be taught not by means of dumb images but by the living preaching of His Word.
right_choice: No. God wants His people taught by living preaching of His Word, not by dumb images.
wrong_choices: The church may use images for instruction, though preaching is also necessary. | Yes, images teach the unlettered laity more effectively than any preaching. | Images may be tolerated in churches but never worshipped or honoured.
basis_note: Habakkuk 2:18-19 calls idols teachers of lies that cannot speak or give guidance, while Romans 10:14 and 17 say faith comes through hearing the preached word of Christ, which supports the answer.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What is required in the third commandment?
answer: We are not to blaspheme or to abuse the Name of God by cursing, perjury, or unnecessary oaths, nor to share in such horrible sins by being silent bystanders. In short, we must use the holy Name of God only with fear and reverence, so that we may rightly confess Him, call upon Him, and praise Him in all our words and works.

question: Is the blaspheming of God's Name by swearing and cursing such a grievous sin that God is angry also with those who do not prevent and forbid it as much as they can?
answer: Certainly, for no sin is greater or provokes God's wrath more than the blaspheming of His Name. That is why He commanded it to be punished with death.
right_choice: Certainly. No sin provokes God's wrath more than blaspheming His Name, which He commanded to be punished with death.
wrong_choices: Yes, but willful murder and idolatry provoke God's wrath far more | Certainly, and God commanded that all blasphemy be punished by exile from the land | No, God is angry only with the one who speaks the blasphemy, not with those who hear it and stay silent
basis_note: Leviticus 24:16 states that whoever blasphemes the LORD's name must be put to death, which supports the answer's claim that God commanded blasphemers to be punished with death. The claim that no sin is greater or provokes more wrath is not stated in the shown verses.
doubt: The superlative "no sin is greater or provokes God's wrath more" is not stated in the shown verses; Leviticus 24:16 shows only the death penalty, and Leviticus 5:1 does not speak of blasphemy.
audit_why: One wrong choice (that blasphemy may be forgiven if the sinner repents) is true to the Bible, so it was replaced with a choice that Leviticus 5:1 contradicts, and a grammar slip in another wrong choice was fixed.

question: But may we swear an oath by the Name of God in a godly manner?
answer: Yes, when the government demands it of its subjects, or when necessity requires it, in order to maintain and promote fidelity and truth, to God's glory and for our neighbour's good. Such oath-taking is based on God's Word and was therefore rightly used by saints in the Old and the New Testament.
right_choice: Yes, when government demands or necessity requires, to maintain truth and fidelity for God's glory and neighbour's good.
wrong_choices: No, for swearing oaths by God's Name shows insufficient faith in His providence and care | Yes, but only in serious court cases where the government requires an oath of truth | No, we should never swear oaths by God's Name, as Jesus Himself forbade this practice
basis_note: Deut 6:13 commands Israel to take oaths in the LORD's name, and Heb 6:16 says oaths confirm and end argument. Saints such as Paul (2 Cor 1:23) swore this way. The government and necessity limits are the answer's own application, not stated in these verses.
audit_why: The catechism teaching and the Bible references fit, but the short right choice was too long and awkwardly worded, so it was tightened to 20 words or fewer without changing its meaning. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The teaching, answer, and choices are accurate and well supported by the listed verses; only the reference's punctuation was changed to the site's standard format.

question: May we also swear by saints or other creatures?
answer: No. A lawful oath is a calling upon God, who alone knows the heart, to bear witness to the truth, and to punish me if I swear falsely. No creature is worthy of such honour.
right_choice: No. Lawful oath calls upon God alone, who knows our heart, to witness truth. No creature deserves such honour.
wrong_choices: No, we should never swear any oath at all, by God or other powers | Yes, we may swear by the saints because God honors those who honor His people | Yes, but only by the angels who serve God and sit upon His throne
basis_note: Christ forbids swearing by heaven, earth, or other creatures (Matt 5:34-37; James 5:12). Swearing by heaven or the temple is really swearing by God who dwells there (Matt 23:21-22). Paul calls God as witness (2 Cor 1:23).
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What does God require in the fourth commandment?
answer: First, that the ministry of the gospel and the schools be maintained and that, especially on the day of rest, I diligently attend the church of God to hear God's Word, to use the sacraments, to call publicly upon the LORD, and to give Christian offerings for the poor. Second, that all the days of my life I rest from my evil works, let the LORD work in me through His Holy Spirit, and so begin in this life the eternal sabbath.

question: What does God require in the fifth commandment?
answer: That I show all honour, love, and faithfulness to my father and mother and to all those in authority over me, submit myself with due obedience to their good instruction and discipline, and also have patience with their weaknesses and shortcomings, since it is God's will to govern us by their hand.
right_choice: Show honour, love, and faithfulness to parents and authorities; obey their instruction; bear their weaknesses; God governs by them.
wrong_choices: Show perfect obedience to parents and follow all their commands without ever questioning judgment | Honor your parents but you need not obey them if you disagree with commands | Show respect to parents but trust your own conscience more than their instruction
basis_note: Children are told to obey parents and to honor them, and everyone is to submit to governing authorities appointed by God. The answer's patience with parents' weaknesses is not stated in these verses.
audit_why: The answer matches the Heidelberg Catechism and the wrong choices are clearly wrong, but the short right choice was 21 words, so I shortened it to 19 while keeping its meaning.

question: What does God require in the sixth commandment?
answer: I am not to dishonour, hate, injure, or kill my neighbour by thoughts, words, or gestures, and much less by deeds, whether personally or through another; rather, I am to put away all desire of revenge. Moreover, I am not to harm or recklessly endanger myself. Therefore, also, the government bears the sword to prevent murder.
right_choice: Not to dishonour, hate, or kill by thought, word, or deed; put away revenge; not harm myself; government prevents murder.
wrong_choices: To avoid only the outward act of murder, since anger and hateful words are not judged under this commandment | To show love to enemies and refrain from defending yourself or others from attack | To refrain from personally killing but permit suffering and harm through your deliberate inaction
verses: Matthew 5:21-22; Leviticus 19:17-18; Romans 12:19; Romans 13:4; Matthew 26:52; Matthew 4:7
basis_note: Matthew 5:21-22 forbids anger, insulting words, and murder; Leviticus 19:17-18 forbids hatred and revenge; Romans 13:4 gives the government the sword; Matthew 4:7 is the only shown verse near self-harm, and it speaks of testing God.
audit_why: One wrong choice (actively protecting a neighbor from harm) is actually part of what the catechism teaches about this commandment, so it was replaced with a clearly wrong one, and the right choice was shortened to fit the word limit.

question: But does this commandment speak only of killing?
answer: By forbidding murder God teaches us that He hates the root of murder, such as envy, hatred, anger, and desire of revenge, and that He regards all these as murder.
right_choice: God forbids the root of murder: envy, hatred, anger, and revenge, which He regards as murder.
wrong_choices: God permits some anger and hatred if they do not result in actual violence | God forbids murder but permits justified anger and revenge against those who harm us | God condemns the act of murder but permits feelings of hatred in one's heart
basis_note: 1 John 3:15 says whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and Matthew 5:22 treats anger and insulting words as liable to judgment. Together they teach that God counts the root sins of hatred and anger as murder.
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer, right choice, and wrong choices are all accurate and well supported by the verses, including 1 John 3:15 and Matthew 5:22, but the reference list was missing Matthew 5:22, which directly supports the point about anger being regarded as murder, so it has been added.

question: Is it enough, then, that we do not kill our neighbour in any such way?
answer: No. God commands us to love our neighbour as ourselves, showing patience, gentleness, mercy, and doing good even to our enemies.
right_choice: No. God commands us to love our neighbour as ourselves, showing patience, gentleness, mercy, and doing good even to our enemies.
wrong_choices: God commands us to show kindness only to those who treat us with respect and kindness | We must love our neighbors but we are not obligated to show mercy to enemies | Yes, if we simply avoid murder and hatred we have fully satisfied God's requirements
basis_note: Scripture commands loving the neighbour as oneself (Matt 22:39), clothing oneself with compassion, gentleness and patience (Col 3:12), and returning an enemy's stray ox or helping his fallen donkey (Exod 23:4-5).
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The teaching and wrong choices hold up against the four confirmed verses, but the reference list was padded with many extra citations beyond what the check could confirm, so it has been trimmed to the four verses that are verified to hold the answer.

question: What does the seventh commandment teach us?
answer: That all unchastity is cursed by God. We must therefore detest it from the heart and live chaste and disciplined lives, both within and outside of holy marriage.

question: Does God in this commandment forbid nothing more than adultery and similar shameful sins?
answer: Since we, body and soul, are temples of the Holy Spirit, it is God's will that we keep ourselves pure and holy. Therefore He forbids all unchaste acts, gestures, words, thoughts, desires, and whatever may entice us to unchastity.
right_choice: Since we are temples of the Holy Spirit, God forbids all unchaste acts, words, thoughts, desires, and whatever entices us to unchastity.
wrong_choices: God forbids outward acts of unchastity and immorality but permits private thoughts and secret desires | God forbids the act of adultery and unchastity but private thoughts and desires are not sinful | The seventh commandment forbids adultery and external unchaste behavior but permits private lustful thoughts alone
basis_note: Matthew 5:28 forbids lustful looking in the heart, 1 Corinthians 6:19 calls the body a temple of the Holy Spirit, and Ephesians 5:3-4 forbids even a hint of impurity, obscenity, or crude joking.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What does God forbid in the eighth commandment?
answer: God forbids not only outright theft and robbery but also such wicked schemes and devices as false weights and measures, deceptive merchandising, counterfeit money, and usury; we must not defraud our neighbour in any way, whether by force or by show of right. In addition God forbids all greed and all abuse or squandering of His gifts.

question: What does God require of you in this commandment?
answer: I must promote my neighbour's good wherever I can and may, deal with him as I would like others to deal with me, and work faithfully so that I may be able to give to those in need.
right_choice: Promote my neighbour's good, treat him as I wish to be treated, work faithfully to give to those in need.
wrong_choices: We should help the poor when they are truly worthy and clearly deserving of our aid | Help your neighbor but do not work excessively hard or earn too much money | Treat others well only when they treat you well and show you kindness first and foremost
basis_note: Matthew 7:12 gives the rule to do to others as you would have them do to you; Ephesians 4:28 says to work and do good so you may share with the needy; Galatians 6:10 says to do good to everyone as opportunity allows.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What is required in the ninth commandment?
answer: I must not give false testimony against anyone, twist no one's words, not gossip or slander, nor condemn or join in condemning anyone rashly and unheard. Rather, I must avoid all lying and deceit as the devil's own works, under penalty of God's heavy wrath. In court and everywhere else, I must love the truth, speak and confess it honestly, and do what I can to defend and promote my neighbour's honour and reputation.

question: What does the tenth commandment require of us?
answer: That not even the slightest thought or desire contrary to any of God's commandments should ever arise in our heart. Rather, we should always hate all sin with all our heart, and delight in all righteousness.
right_choice: No thought or desire against any commandment should arise; hate all sin with all heart and delight in all righteousness.
wrong_choices: Avoid coveting only what belongs to our neighbor, since other desires of the heart do not matter to God | Control your outward actions strictly but recognize private thoughts and desires cannot be regulated | Avoid serious and major sins, but small thoughts of sin are unavoidable and natural
basis_note: The law's command "Do not covet" exposes desire as sin (Rom 7:7), David hates sin with perfect hatred (Ps 139:22), and God's precepts bring joy to the heart (Ps 19:8).
audit_why: One wrong choice described a godly practice (avoid sinful thoughts and confess them), so it could be picked fairly; it was replaced with a clearly wrong choice that limits the commandment to outward coveting.

question: But can those converted to God keep these commandments perfectly?
answer: No. In this life even the holiest have only a small beginning of this obedience. Nevertheless, with earnest purpose they do begin to live not only according to some but to all the commandments of God.
right_choice: No. The holiest have only a small beginning of this obedience, yet earnestly begin to live according to all God's commandments.
wrong_choices: The holiest can keep the most important commandments but will never fully obey them all | Yes, the most holy and righteous believers can keep all God's commandments perfectly in this life | No, and therefore the righteous do not need to seriously try to obey all commandments
basis_note: No one is without sin, and Paul struggles with unfulfilled desire, yet he delights in God's law and presses on toward perfection, so the answer follows from these verses.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: If in this life no one can keep the ten commandments perfectly, why does God have them preached so strictly?
answer: First, that throughout our life we may more and more become aware of our sinful nature, and therefore seek more eagerly the forgiveness of sins and righteousness in Christ. Second, that we may be zealous for good deeds and constantly pray to God for the grace of the Holy Spirit, that He may more and more renew us after God's image, until after this life we reach the goal of perfection.
right_choice: So we see our sin and seek Christ, pursue good deeds and prayer, and grow more in God's image.
wrong_choices: To frighten sinners into strict obedience rather than encourage them toward growth | So we will achieve perfect holiness and complete righteousness through our own human effort | To ensure we feel guilty about our many sins and work harder at righteousness
basis_note: Romans 3:20 says the law brings awareness of sin, and Romans 3:24 says we are justified by grace in Christ. Philippians 3:12-14 describes pressing on toward the goal of perfection, not yet attained.
audit_why: The catechism answer and the wrong choices are sound and match the Bible passages. Only the short right choice was one word too long, so it has been trimmed without changing its meaning.

question: Why is prayer necessary for Christians?
answer: Because prayer is the most important part of the thankfulness which God requires of us. Moreover, God will give His grace and the Holy Spirit only to those who constantly and with heartfelt longing ask Him for these gifts and thank Him for them.
right_choice: Prayer is necessary because it's most important to the thankfulness God requires; He gives grace and Holy Spirit only to those asking constantly.
wrong_choices: Prayer is optional for believers who have already received God's grace and full salvation | Prayer is less important than reading Scripture and performing good works for others | God gives grace and the Holy Spirit according to our own righteousness and merit
basis_note: Psalm 50:14-15 pairs thanksgiving with calling on God in the day of trouble, and Luke 11:13 says the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask. "Most important part" is the catechism's emphasis, not a stated ranking.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What belongs to a prayer which pleases God and is heard by Him?
answer: First, we must from the heart call upon the one true God only, who has revealed Himself in His Word, for all that He has commanded us to pray. Second, we must thoroughly know our need and misery, so that we may humble ourselves before God. Third, we must rest on this firm foundation that, although we do not deserve it, God will certainly hear our prayer for the sake of Christ our Lord, as He has promised us in His Word.
right_choice: Call upon God revealed in His Word; know our need to humble ourselves; trust God hears for Christ's sake.
wrong_choices: Pray with great emotion and feeling; repeat the same words many times; trust our own worthiness to be heard. | Call upon saints as well as God; hide our need from Him; trust God hears for our good works. | Use fancy and beautiful language; ask God for worldly wealth and pleasure; trust our prayer is strong enough.
basis_note: Prayer must call on the Lord in truth and spirit, Daniel humbly pleads not for his righteous acts but for God's compassion, and Jesus promises to answer prayer asked in His name.
audit_why: The catechism answer is sound, but the wrong choices were a jumble of three sets that were too short and made the right choice stand out, so they are now three matching three-part choices, and the reference list is trimmed to the fitting passages. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and wrong choices are sound, but the reference included Romans 8:26-27, which does not support this answer's three points, so the reference was tightened to the verses that actually hold it.

question: What has God commanded us to ask of Him?
answer: All the things we need for body and soul, as included in the prayer which Christ our Lord Himself taught us.
right_choice: All the things we need for body and soul, as included in the prayer which Christ our Lord Himself taught us.
wrong_choices: Only spiritual things for our souls; worldly things like food and shelter are sinful requests. | Only what we truly deserve based on our good works and moral worthiness. | Only material blessings and health; we should never pray for forgiveness or spiritual growth.
basis_note: Jesus says "this is how you should pray" and gives the Lord's Prayer. Its petitions cover bodily need (daily bread) and the soul (forgiveness, deliverance from evil), so the answer follows from it.
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The reference pointed to verses about seeking God's kingdom and good gifts coming from above, but not to the Lord's Prayer that the answer actually describes, so the reference was corrected to Matt 6:9-13 where Christ teaches that very prayer covering both body and soul.

question: What is the Lord's prayer?
answer: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.
right_choice: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come. Give us daily bread, forgive us, and deliver us from the evil one.
wrong_choices: You shall have no other gods before Me. You shall not make for yourself an idol in the form of anything in the heavens above. | I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth, and in Jesus Christ His only Son, our Lord. | Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.
basis_note: Jesus says, "this is how you should pray," then gives the prayer in Matthew 6:9-13, which matches the catechism's answer phrase by phrase.
audit_why: The answer used old KJV wording (\"Thy\", \"art\") and added a closing doxology that is not in the BSB, so it now follows the BSB text of Matthew 6:9-13, and the wrong choices were given modern wording too.

question: Why has Christ commanded us to address God as Our Father?
answer: To awaken in us at the very beginning of our prayer that childlike reverence and trust toward God which should be basic to our prayer: God has become our Father through Christ and will much less deny us what we ask of Him in faith than our fathers would refuse us earthly things.
right_choice: To awaken childlike reverence and trust; God through Christ became our Father and gives us what we ask in faith.
wrong_choices: To show respect to our earthly parents, who are the first representatives of God's authority and care for us. | To establish a formal distance and proper reverence, so we do not presume upon God's holiness with casual familiarity. | To acknowledge God as the Creator and Almighty Maker of all things, whose power transcends all earthly authority.
basis_note: Matthew 7:9-11 teaches that the Father in heaven gives good things to those who ask Him, far more than earthly fathers give to their children. The "childlike reverence" purpose is the catechism's own inference, not stated in these verses.
audit_why: No fault found.
