question: Why is there added, "in heaven" in the words "Our Father in heaven"?
answer: These words teach us not to think of God's heavenly majesty in an earthly manner, and to expect from His almighty power all things we need for body and soul.
right_choice: Not to think of God's majesty in an earthly manner, and to expect all things we need from His almighty power.
wrong_choices: To indicate that God dwells physically in the heavens above and is separated from the earthly realm entirely. | To teach us that we must hope in the heavenly reward awaiting us after death and resurrection. | To remind us of God's perfect government of all things in heaven, but not His rule over earthly matters.
basis_note: God is not only a God nearby but fills heaven and earth, so His heavenly majesty is not earthly; and your heavenly Father knows your needs and will freely give all things, as Matthew 6:32-33 and Romans 8:32 say.
audit_why: The question used the old wording "Who art in heaven"; it now uses the BSB's "Our Father in heaven", and the catechism answer is unchanged.

question: What is the first petition of the Lord's Prayer?
answer: Hallowed be Your name. That is: Grant us first of all that we may rightly know You, and sanctify, glorify, and praise You in all Your works, in which shine forth Your almighty power, wisdom, goodness, righteousness, mercy, and truth. Grant us also that we may so direct our whole life—our thoughts, words, and actions—that Your name is not blasphemed because of us but always honored and praised.
right_choice: That we rightly know God, praise Him in all His works, and live so His name is honored, not blasphemed.
wrong_choices: That God rules us completely and we submit to His will in all earthly matters and spiritual concerns. | That we are forgiven of our sins and our debts are pardoned by God's infinite mercy and compassion. | That God's kingdom grows mightily and rules all nations until His return in glory and power over all things.
basis_note: Matthew 6:9 gives the prayer as "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name," with that petition first, before "Your kingdom come" in verse 10.
audit_why: The answer used old wording ("Thy," "Thee") and the right choice was too long, so both were put in modern BSB-style wording, and Matthew 6:9, where the petition is found, was added to the reference.

question: What is the second petition?
answer: Your kingdom come. That is: So rule us by Your Word and Spirit that more and more we submit to You. Preserve and increase Your church. Destroy the works of the devil, every power that raises itself against You, and every conspiracy against Your holy Word. Do all this until the fullness of Your kingdom comes, in which You will be all in all.
right_choice: God ruling us by His Word and Spirit, preserving His church, destroying the devil's works, until His kingdom comes.
wrong_choices: That God would grant us earthly prosperity, success in our labors, and material abundance as signs of His favor. | That all people everywhere would honor and revere God's holy Name above all else and sing His praises. | That God would provide for us our daily needs for food, shelter, and security in this life.
basis_note: Jesus teaches the prayer "Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven," which is the second petition; the catechism's added explanation draws on its listed proof texts.
audit_why: The answer used old-style words like "Thy," "Thee," and "Thou," so it now uses modern BSB-style wording ("Your kingdom come"), and the teaching and choices are unchanged.

question: What is the third petition?
answer: Thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. That is: Grant that we and all men may deny our own will, and without any murmuring obey Thy will, for it alone is good. Grant also that everyone may carry out the duties of his office and calling as willingly and faithfully as the angels in heaven.

question: What is the fourth petition?
answer: Give us this day our daily bread. That is: Provide us with all our bodily needs so that we may acknowledge that Thou art the only fountain of all good, and that our care and labour, and also Thy gifts, cannot do us any good without Thy blessing. Grant therefore that we may withdraw our trust from all creatures, and place it only in Thee.

question: What is the fifth petition?
answer: And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. That is: For the sake of Christ's blood, do not impute to us, wretched sinners, any of our transgressions, nor the evil which still clings to us, as we also find this evidence of Your grace in us that we are fully determined wholeheartedly to forgive our neighbor.
right_choice: For Christ's blood, do not impute our sins to us; evidence of God's grace is that we wholeheartedly forgive our neighbors.
wrong_choices: For God's justice, do not allow our wickedness to remain; evidence of faith is that we confess all transgressions. | For Christ's sake, grant us strength against temptation; evidence of God's love is that we remain steadfast in His Word. | For God's mercy, forgive all past and future offenses; evidence of grace is that we give abundantly to the poor.
basis_note: Matthew 6:12 states the fifth petition: "And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors." The catechism's added explanation rests on the other shown passages, such as Romans 8:1 and 1 John 2:1-2.
audit_why: The answer used the old-style "Thy grace", which is now "Your grace" to match the BSB, a stray semicolon was removed, and the reference now includes Matthew 6:12, where the petition itself appears.

question: What is the sixth petition?
answer: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. That is: In ourselves we are so weak that we cannot stand even for a moment. Moreover, our sworn enemies-- the devil, the world, and our own flesh-- do not cease to attack us. Will You, therefore, uphold and strengthen us by the power of Your Holy Spirit, so that in this spiritual war we may not go down to defeat, but always firmly resist our enemies, until we finally obtain the complete victory.
right_choice: Ask God to strengthen us by His Holy Spirit, since we are too weak to resist our enemies.
wrong_choices: Ask God to deliver us from all physical evil and to grant us prosperity and health in earthly life. | Ask God to remove all difficult circumstances and trials that test our faith and commitment to His Word. | Ask God to prevent us from knowing sin and to keep us entirely free from all spiritual warfare.
basis_note: Matthew 6:13 gives the petition itself: "And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one." The printed answer's explanation draws on the question's reference verses, such as Ephesians 6 and 1 Peter 5:8.
audit_why: The answer used old-fashioned words ("Wilt Thou", "Thy"), so it now reads "Will You" and "Your", and the right choice is shortened to fit the length limit.

question: How do you conclude your prayer?
answer: For yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever. That is: All this we ask of You because, as our King, having power over all things, You are both willing and able to give us all that is good, and because not we but Your holy name should receive all glory forever.
right_choice: For yours is the kingdom, power, and glory forever. You are King over all, willing and able to grant our requests.
wrong_choices: According to your will, O Lord, submitting all our requests to God's sovereign wisdom and perfect purpose. | Give us this day our daily bread, asking God to provide everything we need for body and life. | Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors, trusting in God's mercy toward sinners.
basis_note: The closing words are the doxology, which the BSB's Matthew 6:13 omits (it ends at "the evil one"); it is a later addition absent from the earliest manuscripts. Psalm 115:1 and Romans 10:12 support the explanation.
doubt: The printed answer gives the doxology as the conclusion, but no shown verse contains those words; the BSB text of Matthew 6:13 ends before them.
audit_why: The answer and choices used old KJV-style words (Thine, Thee, Thou), and two wrong choices ("Amen" and "In the Name of Jesus Christ") could also be fair ways to close a prayer, so the wording was modernized and those two were replaced with petitions of the Lord's Prayer.

question: What does the word Amen mean?
answer: Amen means: It is true and certain. For God has much more certainly heard my prayer than I feel in my heart that I desire this of Him.
right_choice: It is true and certain; God has more certainly heard my prayer than I feel my desire in my heart.
wrong_choices: The end of prayer, signifying that we have completed our petitions and are finished addressing God. | Hallelujah, a cry of praise giving glory to God for all the good He has done for us. | Let the covenant be sealed, confirming the binding agreement between God and His people.
basis_note: No shown verse defines Amen as "true and certain"; that meaning comes from the Hebrew word's sense of firmness. The second sentence rests on Isaiah 65:24, where God hears before people call.
audit_why: One wrong choice ("So be it done...") is nearly the usual meaning of Amen and could fairly be picked, so it was replaced with a clearly wrong one; the rest is unchanged.

question: What do the scriptures principally teach?
answer: The scriptures principally teach, what man is to believe concerning God, and what duty God requires of man.

question: Are there more Gods than one?
answer: There is but one only, the living and true God.
right_choice: There is but one only, the living and true God.
wrong_choices: There are no Gods; only the forces of nature that we call divine and eternal principles. | There are three Gods: God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit equal in power. | There are many gods, and the LORD is only the greatest among them all.
basis_note: Deuteronomy 6:4 says the LORD is One, and Jeremiah 10:10 calls the LORD the true God and the living God, so the answer that there is one only, living and true God is stated.
audit_why: The first wrong choice was mostly true (the nations' gods are not the true God), so it was replaced with a choice that plainly contradicts the teaching that there is one God.

question: Into what estate did the fall bring mankind?
answer: The fall brought mankind into an estate of sin and misery.

question: What is the duty which God requireth of man?
answer: The duty which God requireth of man, is obedience to his revealed will.

question: Which is the third commandment?
answer: The third commandment is, Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain: for the Lord will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.

question: Which is the fourth commandment?
answer: The fourth commandment is, Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labor, and do all thy work: but the seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates: For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day: wherefore the Lord blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it.

question: Which is the sixth commandment?
answer: The sixth commandment is, Thou shalt not kill.

question: Which is the seventh commandment?
answer: The seventh commandment is, Thou shalt not commit adultery.

question: Which is the eighth commandment?
answer: The eighth commandment is, You shall not steal.
right_choice: The eighth commandment is, You shall not steal.
wrong_choices: The eighth commandment is, Honor your father and your mother. | The eighth commandment is, You shall not commit adultery. | The eighth commandment is, You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.
basis_note: Exodus 20:15 gives the words "You shall not steal," which is the eighth of the ten commandments in the order of Exodus 20:2-17.
audit_why: The answer and choices used old KJV-style wording ("Thou shalt"), so they were reworded to the BSB ("You shall not steal"), and the reference was tidied.

question: What is the chief and highest end of man?
answer: Man's chief and highest end is to glorify God, and fully to enjoy him forever.

question: How doth it appear that there is a God?
answer: The very light of nature in man, and the works of God, declare plainly that there is a God; but his word and Spirit only do sufficiently and effectually reveal him unto men for their salvation.

question: What is the word of God?
answer: The holy scriptures of the Old and New Testaments are the word of God, the only rule of faith and obedience.

question: How doth it appear that the scriptures are the word of God?
answer: The scriptures manifest themselves to be the word of God, by their majesty and purity; by the consent of all the parts, and the scope of the whole, which is to give all glory to God; by their light and power to convince and convert sinners, to comfort and build up believers unto salvation: but the Spirit of God bearing witness by and with the scriptures in the heart of man, is alone able fully to persuade it that they are the very word of God.

question: What do the scriptures make known of God?
answer: The scriptures make known what God is, the persons in the Godhead, his decrees, and the execution of his decrees.
right_choice: The scriptures make known what God is, the persons in the Godhead, his decrees, and the execution of them.
wrong_choices: The scriptures make known God's laws and commandments, the stories of the prophets, and lives of the apostles. | The scriptures make known what God requires of us, how He forgave all sins, and how we should live. | The scriptures make known God's love for mankind, the history of Israel, and predictions about the future.
basis_note: Matthew 28:19 names the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; Acts 4:28 shows God's decided purpose being carried out; Hebrews 11:6 shows that God exists and rewards those who seek Him.
audit_why: The answer matches the Larger Catechism, but the proof text 1 John 5:7 relies on KJV wording that the BSB lacks, so Matthew 28:19 (Father, Son and Holy Spirit) replaces it.

question: What is God?
answer: God is a Spirit, in and of himself infinite in being, glory, blessedness, and perfection; all-sufficient, eternal, unchangeable, incomprehensible, everywhere present, almighty, knowing all things, most wise, most holy, most just, most merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth.

question: How many persons are there in the Godhead?
answer: There be three persons in the Godhead, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost; and these three are one true, eternal God, the same in substance, equal in power and glory; although distinguished by their personal properties.

question: What are the personal properties of the three persons in the Godhead?
answer: It is proper to the Father to beget the Son, and to the Son to be begotten of the Father, and to the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father and the Son from all eternity.
right_choice: The Father begets the Son, the Son is begotten of the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from both eternally.
wrong_choices: The Father is almighty and eternal, the Son is our Redeemer and mediator, and the Holy Spirit is our comforter and guide. | The Father made the heavens and earth, the Son became incarnate and died for our sins, and the Spirit sanctifies believers. | The Father is the source of all things, the Son reveals the Father's will, and the Spirit applies redemption to believers.
basis_note: Hebrews 1:5 shows the Father begetting the Son, John 15:26 the Spirit proceeding from the Father, and Galatians 4:6 the Spirit sent as the Son's Spirit. "From all eternity" is a theological gloss not stated in these verses.
audit_why: The answer said "Holy Ghost", which is KJV wording, so it now says "Holy Spirit" as the BSB does and as the wrong choices already did. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and choices are sound and supported by Hebrews 1:5, John 15:26, and Galatians 4:6, but the reference was pared down to just those three verses since the extra ones were not confirmed to hold the answer.

question: How does it appear that the Son and the Holy Spirit are God equal with the Father?
answer: The Scriptures show that the Son and the Holy Spirit are God equal with the Father, ascribing to them such names, attributes, works, and worship as are proper to God only.
right_choice: Scripture ascribes to the Son and the Spirit God's proper names, attributes, works, and worship.
wrong_choices: They are called god-like beings but are subordinate to the Father and derive their powers from Him. | They possess some divine attributes like wisdom and power but not full equality with the Father. | The Bible distinguishes three different levels of divine being, with the Father supreme and the others lesser.
basis_note: The Word, who is the Son, is called God (John 1:1). Lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God (Acts 5:4). All things were created through the Son (Col 1:16). Baptism is in the one name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matt 28:19).
audit_why: The catechism's teaching is right, but the question and answer used old wording ("doth", "Holy Ghost", "unto"), so I changed them to modern BSB-style wording and shortened the right choice to fit the length limit.

question: What are the decrees of God?
answer: God's decrees are the wise, free, and holy acts of the counsel of his will, whereby, from all eternity, he hath, for his own glory, unchangeably foreordained: Whatsoever comes to pass in time, especially concerning angels and men.

question: What hath God especially decreed concerning angels and men?
answer: God, by an eternal and immutable decree, out of his mere love, for the praise of his glorious grace, to be manifested in due time, hath elected some angels to glory; and in Christ hath chosen some men to eternal life, and the means thereof: and also, according to his sovereign power, and the unsearchable counsel of his own will (whereby he extendeth or withholdeth favor as he pleases), hath passed by and foreordained the rest to dishonor and wrath, to be for their sin inflicted, to the praise of the glory of his justice.
right_choice: God eternally elected some angels to glory and some men to eternal life in Christ, and foreordained others to wrath.
wrong_choices: God chose some to be His covenant people based on His foreknowledge of their goodness and righteousness. | God foresaw who would believe in Christ and predestined only those who exercise faith to salvation and eternal life. | God elected all people to salvation through Christ and earnestly desires that none should perish but all be saved.
basis_note: Ephesians 1:4-5 shows God choosing and predestining people before the world's foundation, Romans 9:18 shows His choosing whom He wills, Romans 9:22 shows vessels of wrath, and 1 Timothy 5:21 names elect angels.
doubt: The shown verses speak of elect angels but do not state that other angels were passed by, so that part of the answer is inferred rather than stated.
audit_why: The catechism teaching and choices are sound, but the right choice was a little too long, so it was shortened slightly to keep the same meaning.

question: How doth God execute his decrees?
answer: God executeth his decrees in the works of creation and providence, according to his infallible foreknowledge, and the free and immutable counsel of his own will.

question: What is the work of creation?
answer: The work of creation is that wherein God did in the beginning, by the word of his power, make of nothing the world, and all things therein, for himself, within the space of six days, and all very good.

question: How did God create angels?
answer: God created all the angels spirits, immortal, holy, excelling in knowledge, mighty in power, to execute his commandments, and to praise his name, yet subject to change.
right_choice: God created angels immortal, holy spirits of knowledge and power, to execute commandments and praise God, yet subject to change.
wrong_choices: God created angels as pure spirits composed of divine substance, eternal and unchangeable like God Himself. | God fashioned the angels from the dust of the earth as He did man, but gave them spiritual bodies. | God caused the angels to evolve from lower creatures over time, perfecting them into spiritual beings of great power.
basis_note: Col 1:16 says all things, including thrones and dominions, were created; Heb 1:14 calls angels spirits; Ps 103:20-21 gives their strength, obedience and praise; Luke 20:36 says they cannot die; Luke 9:26 calls them holy; 2 Pet 2:4 shows they could sin and change.
audit_why: The catechism answer and wrong choices are sound, but the short right choice was one word over the length limit, so I trimmed one word and kept its meaning. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer, right choice, and wrong choices are all sound, but the reference list cited verses that don't clearly support the answer in the BSB wording and left out verses that do; the reference has been corrected to the full set of verses that actually hold each part of the answer.

question: How did God create man?
answer: After God had made all other creatures, he created man male and female; formed the body of the man of the dust of the ground, and the woman of the rib of the man, endued them with living, reasonable, and immortal souls; made them after his own image, in knowledge, righteousness,and holiness; having the law of God written in their hearts, and power to fulfil it, and dominion over the creatures; yet subject to fall.

question: What are God's works of providence?
answer: God's works of providence are his most holy, wise, and powerful preserving and governing all his creatures; ordering them, and all their actions, to his own glory.

question: What is God's providence towards the angels?
answer: God by his providence permitted some of the angels, wilfully and irrecoverably, to fall into sin and damnation, limiting and ordering that, and all their sins, to his own glory; and established the rest in holiness and happiness; employing them all, at his pleasure, in the administrations of his power, mercy, and justice.
right_choice: God permitted some angels to fall willfully into sin and damnation; He established the rest in holiness and employs both to His glory.
wrong_choices: God permitted all angels to fall willfully into sin and damnation; He employs them to bring glory to Satan. | God prevented some angels from falling into sin and damnation; the rest fell and are employed in judgment. | God permitted some angels to fall through temptation and weakness; He established the rest but employs some unwillingly.
basis_note: Jude 1:6 and 2 Peter 2:4 show angels who sinned kept in chains for judgment, Job 1:12 shows God limiting Satan, and Hebrews 1:14 shows angels sent to serve. Ordering all their sins to God's glory is inference.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What was the providence of God toward man in the estate in which he was created?
answer: The providence of God toward man in the estate in which he was created, was the placing him in paradise, appointing him to dress it, giving him liberty to eat of the fruit of the earth; putting the creatures under his dominion, and ordaining marriage for his help; affording him communion with himself; instituting the sabbath; entering into a covenant of life with him, upon condition of personal, perfect, and perpetual obedience, of which the tree of life was a pledge; and forbidding to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, upon the pain of death.

question: Did man continue in that estate wherein God at first created him?
answer: Our first parents being left to the freedom of their own will, through the temptation of Satan, transgressed the commandment of God in eating the forbidden fruit; and thereby fell from the estate of innocency wherein they were created.

question: Did all mankind fall in that first transgression ?
answer: The covenant being made with Adam as a public person, not for himself only, but for his posterity, all mankind descending from him by ordinary generation, sinned in him, and fell with him in that first transgression.

question: What is sin?
answer: Sin is any want of conformity unto, or transgression of, any law of God, given as a rule to the reasonable creature.

question: Wherein consists the sinfulness of that estate whereinto man fell?
answer: The sinfulness of that estate whereinto man fell, consisteth in the guilt of Adam's first sin, the want of that righteousness wherein he was created, and the corruption of his nature, whereby he is utterly indisposed, disabled, and made opposite unto all that is spiritually good, and wholly inclined to all evil, and that continually; which is commonly called Original Sin, and from which do proceed all actual transgressions.

question: How is original sin conveyed from our first parents unto their posterity?
answer: Original sin is conveyed from our first parents unto their posterity by natural generation, so as all that proceed from them in that way are conceived and born in sin.
right_choice: Original sin passes from our first parents through natural generation to all their descendants conceived and born in sin.
wrong_choices: Only to those who consciously imitate their disobedience and reject God's covenant as they did. | Through the example and influence of the sinful lifestyle that they established and taught their children. | By God adding sin to each new soul at its creation, with no link to birth from Adam.
basis_note: Psalm 51:5 says David was sinful from conception, and John 3:6 says flesh is born of flesh, so sin passes through natural birth from parents.
audit_why: One wrong choice spoke of "inheriting the corruption," which is too close to the catechism's own answer, so it was replaced with a choice that clearly denies the link of birth from Adam.

question: What misery did the fall bring upon mankind?
answer: The fall brought upon mankind the loss of communion with God, his displeasure and curse; so as we are by nature children of wrath, bond slaves to Satan, and justly liable to all punishments in this world, and that which is to come.

question: What are the punishments of sin in this world?
answer: The punishments of sin in this world are either inward, as blindness of mind, a reprobate sense, strong delusions, hardness of heart, horror of conscience, and vile affections; or outward, as the curse of God upon the creatures for our sakes, and all other evils that befall us in our bodies, names, estates, relations, and employments; together with death itself.
right_choice: Inward: blindness of mind, hardness of heart; outward: God's curse on creation, bodily evils, and death.
wrong_choices: Physical sufferings, disease, poverty, loss of loved ones, and shortness of life approaching death. | Separation from family and community in this life, though with inner peace from knowing God. | Spiritual blindness and deepening despair in the soul, until physical death comes as relief.
basis_note: Inward punishments appear as darkened understanding and hardened hearts (Eph 4:18), a depraved mind and vile passions (Rom 1:26, 28), strong delusion (2 Thess 2:11), and terror of conscience (Isa 33:14). Outward ones are the cursed ground (Gen 3:17), bodily and family curses (Deut 28:15-18), and death (Rom 6:23).
audit_why: The catechism answer is faithfully given, but the short right choice was too long and awkward, so it now sums up the inward and outward punishments more briefly and clearly. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and choices are sound, but the reference listed extra verses (Rom 2:5, Gen 4:13, Matt 27:4, Rom 6:21) not among those confirmed to hold the answer, so the reference is trimmed to the verses that actually support it.

question: What are the punishments of sin in the world to come?
answer: The punishments of sin in the world to come are everlasting separation from the comfortable presence of God, and most grievous torments in soul and body, without intermission, in hell fire forever.
right_choice: Everlasting separation from God's comfortable presence and most grievous torments in soul and body, without intermission, in hell fire forever.
wrong_choices: Eternal sleep and unconsciousness as the soul's annihilation, ceasing to exist after physical death. | Temporary punishment followed by restoration and eventual reconciliation with God after suffering is satisfied. | Separation from God's presence without active torment, in darkness and silence but without positive pain.
basis_note: 2 Thessalonians 1:9 gives eternal destruction and separation from the Lord's presence; Mark 9:48 and Revelation 20:10 give fire that is never quenched and torment day and night forever.
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The reference cited Mark 9:44 and 9:46, verses that do not exist in the BSB text (it goes 43,45,47,48), so it was corrected to the three verses that actually hold the catechism's answer: 2 Thess 1:9, Mark 9:48, and Rev 20:10.

question: Doth God leave all mankind to perish in the estate of sin and misery?
answer: God doth not leave all men to perish in the estate of sin and misery, into which they fell by the breach of the first covenant, commonly called the Covenant of Works; but of his mere love and mercy delivereth his elect out of it, and bringeth them into an estate of salvation by the second covenant, commonly called the Covenant of Grace.

question: With whom was the covenant of grace made?
answer: The covenant of grace was made with Christ as the second Adam, and in him with all the elect as his seed.
right_choice: The covenant of grace was made with Christ as the second Adam, and in him with all the elect as his seed.
wrong_choices: The covenant of grace was made with Abraham and his descendants; it was renewed with the people of Israel. | The covenant of grace was made with all believers who trust in Jesus Christ as their personal Savior. | The covenant of grace was made with all humanity; God offers salvation freely to anyone who will accept it.
basis_note: Galatians 3:16 identifies the promised "seed" as Christ, and Romans 5:18-19 presents Christ as the one man whose obedience makes "the many" righteous, as Adam's sin made many sinners.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: How is the grace of God manifested in the second covenant?
answer: The grace of God is manifested in the second covenant, in that he freely provideth and offereth to sinners a Mediator, and life and salvation by him; and requiring faith as the condition to interest them in him, promiseth and giveth his Holy Spirit to all his elect, to work in them that faith, with all other saving graces; and to enable them unto all holy obedience, as the evidence of the truth of their faith and thankfulness to God, and as the way which he hath appointed them to salvation.
right_choice: God freely provides a Mediator and life and salvation by Him; He gives His Holy Spirit to work faith in believers and enable holy obedience.
wrong_choices: God provides a Mediator; believers must work to receive faith through their own efforts and holy obedience. | God gives His Holy Spirit only to those who work righteousness and demonstrate faith through good deeds. | God freely provides salvation through promises; believers must receive faith and achieve holiness through moral discipline.
basis_note: God gives His Son so that whoever believes has eternal life (John 3:16), Christ is the mediator of the new covenant (Heb 9:15), God puts His Spirit within His people to cause obedience (Ezek 36:27), and faith is God's gift (Eph 2:8).
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and wrong choices are sound against John 3:16, Hebrews 9:15, Ezekiel 36:27, and Ephesians 2:8, so only the reference was tightened to these four verses, which together do hold the whole answer, instead of the longer list of proof texts that did not each support it on their own.

question: Was the covenant of grace always administered after one and the same manner?
answer: The covenant of grace was not always administered after the same manner, but the administrations of it under the Old Testament were different from those under the New.
right_choice: The covenant of grace was not always administered the same way; Old Testament administrations differed from New Testament administrations.
wrong_choices: There was one unified administration from Abraham onward, though Christ brought fuller revelation and truth. | The covenant itself changed; the administration remained the same throughout the Old and New Testaments. | The substance changed though the outward signs and sacraments remained similar in their basic form.
basis_note: Paul contrasts the new covenant ministry of the Spirit with the earlier ministry of Moses, engraved on stone, calling it a ministry of death and condemnation. The administrations differ, though the verses never name "covenant of grace" outright.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: How was the covenant of grace administered under the Old Testament?
answer: The covenant of grace was administered under the Old Testament, by promises, prophecies, sacrifices, circumcision, the passover, and other types and ordinances, which did all foresignify Christ then to come, and were for that time sufficient to build up the elect in faith in the promised Messiah, by whom they then had full remission of sin, and eternal salvation.
right_choice: By promises, prophecies, sacrifices, circumcision, the passover and types pointing to Christ, sufficient for full remission and salvation.
wrong_choices: By the moral law and keeping God's commandments perfectly, which would secure their righteousness and salvation. | Through sacrifices only, which never truly provided actual forgiveness but only covered sin temporarily. | By types and figures as shadows, but no actual grace was given until Christ's coming.
basis_note: The law's sacrifices and ordinances are a shadow of the coming good things, circumcision is a seal of faith, Christ is the Passover lamb, prophets proclaimed these days, and redemption from Old Covenant transgressions came through Christ's death.
audit_why: The catechism answer is right and the wrong choices contradict it, but the short right choice was over the word limit, so I shortened it and tidied the reference format.

question: How is the covenant of grace administered under the New Testament?
answer: Under the New Testament, when Christ the substance was exhibited, the same covenant of grace was and still is to be administered in the preaching of the word, and the administration of the sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper; in which grace and salvation are held forth in more fulness, evidence, and efficacy, to all nations.
right_choice: By preaching the Word and administering Baptism and Lord's Supper; grace and salvation are held forth in fuller evidence and efficacy to all nations.
wrong_choices: Primarily through the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit in the believer's heart and conscience. | Through preaching alone; the sacraments are merely memorial signs without real efficacy or grace. | By the sacraments only, with preaching as secondary support for the grace they convey.
basis_note: Christ commands the gospel be preached to every creature and disciples be made of all nations by baptizing, and the Lord's Supper is instituted as the new covenant in His blood; 2 Corinthians 3 and Hebrews 8 describe this ministry as better and more glorious.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: Who is the Mediator of the covenant of grace?
answer: The only Mediator of the covenant of grace is the Lord Jesus Christ, who, being the eternal Son of God, of one substance and equal with the Father, in the fulness of time became man, and so was and continues to be God and man, in two entire distinct natures, and one person, forever.
right_choice: The Lord Jesus Christ, eternal Son of God, equal with the Father, is the sole Mediator of the covenant of grace.
wrong_choices: The church and its ordained ministers, who stand as mediators between God and individual believers in hearing confessions. | Moses and the prophets, through whom God mediated His covenant to the Old Testament people of Israel. | The Holy Spirit, who applies the grace of Christ to believers and mediates between God and the church through spiritual gifts.
basis_note: 1 Timothy 2:5 names the one mediator as the man Christ Jesus, and Hebrews 9:15 calls Christ the mediator of the new covenant. John 1:14 and Colossians 2:9 show the Son as God becoming flesh, with the fullness of Deity dwelling in bodily form.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: How did Christ, being the Son of God, become man?
answer: Christ the Son of God became man, by taking to himself a true body, and a reasonable soul, being conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost in the womb of the virgin Mary, of her substance, and born of her, yet without sin.

question: Why was it requisite that the Mediator should be God?
answer: It was requisite that the Mediator should be God, that he might sustain and keep the human nature from sinking under the infinite wrath of God, and the power of death; give worth and efficacy to his sufferings, obedience, and intercession; and to satisfy God's justice, procure his favor, purchase a peculiar people, give his Spirit to them, conquer all their enemies, and bring them to everlasting salvation.
right_choice: God's Mediator must be God to sustain human nature under wrath, give worth to His sacrifice, satisfy justice, and bring salvation.
wrong_choices: A god-like being possessing great divine power would suffice to satisfy God's justice adequately. | Divine nature was needed only to enable Him to rise from death and overcome Satan. | So that He could share in our weakness and be able to suffer and die in our place.
verses: Hebrews 9:14; Titus 2:13-14; Acts 2:24; Hebrews 7:25; Acts 20:28; Romans 3:25
basis_note: Scripture shows the Mediator's divine worth: his eternal Spirit gives his sacrifice worth (Heb 9:14), he is "our great God and Savior" (Titus 2:13), and death could not hold him (Acts 2:24).
audit_why: One wrong choice repeated the catechism's own first reason (keeping His human nature from being crushed), so I replaced it with a reason the catechism gives for His being man, not God.

question: Why was it requisite that the Mediator should be man?
answer: It was requisite that the Mediator should be man, that he might advance our nature, perform obedience to the law, suffer and make intercession for us in our nature, have a fellow feeling of our infirmities; that we might receive the adoption of sons, and have comfort and access with boldness unto the throne of grace.
right_choice: The Mediator must be man to obey the law, suffer and intercede for us, and give us access to God's grace.
wrong_choices: Only as a man could He teach the true way of righteousness to His followers. | He must be man to keep His nature from sinking under God's wrath and to conquer all our enemies. | He must be man to give worth and efficacy to His sufferings and to give His Spirit to His people.
basis_note: Christ was born of a woman and under the law to redeem those under the law, sharing our flesh and blood, made like His brothers to be a merciful high priest, and tempted as we are yet without sin, so we may approach boldly.
audit_why: Two wrong choices (being tempted as we are, and sympathy with human weakness) are actually part of the catechism's answer, so they were replaced with reasons the catechism gives for the Mediator being God.

question: Why was it requisite that the Mediator should be God and man in one person?
answer: It was requisite that the Mediator, who was to reconcile God and man, should himself be both God and man, and this in one person, that the proper works of each nature might be accepted of God for us, and relied on by us, as the works of the whole person.
right_choice: So the works of His divine and human natures are accepted by God for us.
wrong_choices: So the human part could achieve perfection and the divine part ensure complete righteousness. | So He could be honored by both God and humans, being part of both groups. | To show that God and man are essentially the same and equal in nature.
basis_note: Hebrews 9:14 shows one person, Christ, offering himself through the eternal Spirit to cleanse our consciences; Matthew 1:23 names that one person "God with us." The answer follows from these.
audit_why: The catechism answer and the wrong choices are sound, but the right choice was too long, so it was shortened to keep the same teaching, and a stray space in the question was removed.

question: Why was our Mediator called Jesus?
answer: Our Mediator was called Jesus, because he saves his people from their sins.
right_choice: Our Mediator was called Jesus, because he saves his people from their sins.
wrong_choices: Our Mediator was called Jesus, because he taught His disciples the way to eternal life and righteousness. | Our Mediator was called Jesus, because he is our Lord and King who rules over all nations. | Our Mediator was called Jesus, because he heals the sick and performs mighty works and miracles.
basis_note: Matthew 1:21 states the name Jesus is given "because He will save His people from their sins," which matches the answer directly.
audit_why: The answer used the old-fashioned \"saveth\" instead of the BSB's modern wording, so it now reads \"saves\"; the teaching and the wrong choices are unchanged.

question: Why was our Mediator called Christ?
answer: Our Mediator was called Christ, because he was anointed with the Holy Ghost above measure; and so set apart, and fully furnished with all authority and ability, to execute the offices of prophet, priest, and king of his church, in the estate both of his humiliation and exaltation.

question: How doth Christ execute the office of a prophet?
answer: Christ executeth the office of a prophet, in his revealing to the church, in all ages, by his Spirit and word, in divers ways of administration, the whole will of God, in all things concerning their edification and salvation.

question: How doth Christ execute the office of a priest?
answer: Christ executeth the office of a priest, in his once offering himself a sacrifice without spot to God, to be a reconciliation for the sins of his people; and in making continual intercession for them.

question: How doth Christ execute the office of a king?
answer: Christ executeth the office of a king, in calling out of the world a people to himself, and giving them officers, laws, and censures, by which he visibly governs them; in bestowing saving grace upon his elect, rewarding their obedience, and correcting them for their sins, preserving and supporting them under all their temptations and sufferings, restraining and overcoming all their enemies, and powerfully ordering all things for his own glory, and their good; and also in taking vengeance on the rest, who know not God, and obey not the gospel.

question: What was the estate of Christ's humiliation?
answer: The estate of Christ's humiliation was that low condition, wherein he for our sakes, emptying himself of his glory, took upon him the form of a servant, in his conception and birth, life, death, and after his death, until his resurrection.
right_choice: That low condition wherein Christ, emptying Himself of glory, took the form of a servant from conception through death until resurrection.
wrong_choices: His exalted state wherein Christ is advanced to the highest favor with God, possessing all power and glory in heaven and earth. | His miracles and mighty works by which He demonstrated His divine power and authority over sickness, demons, and nature. | His role as prophet, priest, and king, in which He teaches God's will, offers Himself as sacrifice, and rules creation.
basis_note: Philippians 2:6-8 has Christ emptying himself, taking the form of a servant, and dying on a cross; Luke 1:31 gives his conception and birth; Acts 2:24 shows God raising him from death.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: How did Christ humble himself in his conception and birth?
answer: Christ humbled himself in his conception and birth, in that, being from all eternity the Son of God, at the Father's side, he was pleased in the fulness of time to become the son of man, made of a woman of low estate, and to be born of her; with divers circumstances of more than ordinary abasement.
right_choice: From eternity the Son of God at the Father's side, He became son of man, made of a woman of low estate, born in abasement.
wrong_choices: From eternity the Son of God, He became son of man, made of a woman of high estate, born in a palace. | Created before all worlds as the first of the angels, He took flesh from a priestly woman and was born in honor. | Becoming the Son of God at His birth, He was made of a woman of royal rank and born in Jerusalem with great honor.
basis_note: The eternal Son at the Father's side becomes flesh (John 1:14, 1:18), is born of a woman (Gal 4:4), and is laid in a manger with no room in the inn (Luke 2:7).
audit_why: Two wrong choices described things that are true of Christ's birth (the virgin birth, Mary's faithfulness, visitors), so they are replaced with choices that clearly contradict the catechism's teaching of His humble birth. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and right choice used the KJV phrase 'bosom of the Father' for John 1:18, which the BSB renders 'at the Father's side'; this was corrected while the rest of the catechism's teaching was kept.

question: How did Christ humble himself in his life?
answer: Christ humbled himself in his life, by subjecting himself to the law, which he perfectly fulfilled; and by conflicting with the indignities of the world, temptations of Satan, and infirmities in his flesh, whether common to the nature of man, or particularly accompanying that his low condition.
right_choice: By subjecting Himself to the law and perfectly fulfilling it; by conflicting with the world's indignities, Satan's temptations, and infirmities.
wrong_choices: By fulfilling only the ceremonial law; by enduring worldly suffering, demonic opposition, and natural human limitations. | By exempting Himself from the law's requirements and displaying divine power; by conquering worldly indignities without temptation. | By demonstrating perfect obedience to tradition and society; by avoiding Satan's temptations and remaining separate from human weakness.
basis_note: Christ was born under the law (Gal 4:4) and came to fulfill it (Matt 5:17), was tempted by the devil (Matt 4:1-11), endured hostility from sinners (Heb 12:3), and was tempted in every way we are (Heb 4:15).
audit_why: The answer matches the catechism and the Bible texts, but the short right choice was one word too long, so I trimmed it ("human" removed). Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The content of the question, answer, and choices is sound and matches all the cited verses, but the reference list's citation style (periods instead of colons) and an extra verse (Matt 4:12) outside the temptation account were corrected.

question: How did Christ humble himself in his death?
answer: Christ humbled himself in his death, in that having been betrayed by Judas, forsaken by his disciples, scorned and rejected by the world, condemned by Pilate, and tormented by his persecutors; having also conflicted with the terrors of death, and the powers of darkness, felt and borne the weight of God's wrath, he laid down his life an offering for sin, enduring the painful, shameful, and cursed death of the cross.
right_choice: Betrayed, forsaken, rejected, condemned, and tormented, he bore God's wrath and died the painful, shameful, cursed death of the cross.
wrong_choices: He suffered great physical pain and shame, yet remained spiritually exalted and comforted by the Father. | He endured Roman torture and humiliation, but was sustained and comforted by God's constant presence. | He experienced rejection and cruelty from men, but conquered death inwardly and spiritually through His Spirit.
reference: Matt 27:4; Matt 26:56; Isa 53:3; Matt 27:26; Matt 27:30; Luke 22:44; Matt 27:46; Isa 53:10; Phil 2:8; Gal 3:13
verses: Matt 27:4; Matt 26:56; Isa 53:3; Matt 27:26; Matt 27:30; Luke 22:44; Matt 27:46; Isa 53:10; Phil 2:8; Gal 3:13
basis_note: The verses show each part: Judas's betrayal, the disciples fleeing, Christ despised and rejected, Pilate's sentence and the mockery and beating, anguish in Gethsemane, forsaken by God, a guilt offering, death on a cross, and the curse of the cross.
audit_why: The catechism answer and the wrong choices were sound, but the short right choice was too long (24 words), so it was reworded to 20 words with the same teaching. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and choices are sound and match the catechism and the passages, but the listed reference included verses (Isa 53:2, Matt 27:26-50 range, John 19:34, Heb 12:2) not among those verified to hold the answer, so the reference was corrected to the exact set of verses that support it.

question: Wherein consisted Christ's humiliation after his death?
answer: Christ's humiliation after his death consisted in his being buried, and continuing in the state of the dead, and under the power of death till the third day; which hath been otherwise expressed in these words, he descended into hell.
right_choice: Christ was buried and remained under death's power for three days; expressed as 'He descended into hell.'
wrong_choices: Christ's humiliation ended at death; after death He entered glory and ceased to suffer for mankind. | Christ's body was laid in a tomb and His soul went to paradise; He was not truly dead but sleeping. | Christ was buried, and His soul suffered the torments of the damned in hell until the third day.
basis_note: Christ was buried and raised on the third day (1 Cor 15:4), and His soul was not abandoned to Hades nor His body to decay (Acts 2:31). Together these teach burial, continuing among the dead, until the third day.
audit_why: One wrong choice said almost the same as the catechism's answer (buried, in Hades until the third day), so I replaced it with a clearly wrong one, that Christ's soul suffered the torments of the damned.

question: What was the estate of Christ's exaltation?
answer: The estate of Christ's exaltation comprehendeth his resurrection, ascension, sitting at the right hand of the Father, and his coming again to judge the world.

question: How was Christ exalted in his resurrection?
answer: Christ was exalted in his resurrection, in that, not having seen corruption in death (of which it was not possible for him to be held), and having the very same body in which he suffered, with the essential properties thereof (but without mortality, and other common infirmities belonging to this life), really united to his soul, he rose again from the dead the third day by his own power; whereby he declared himself to be the Son of God, to have satisfied divine justice, to have vanquished death, and him that had the power of it, and to be Lord of quick and dead: all which he did as a public person, the head of his church, for their justification, quickening in grace, support against enemies, and to assure them of their resurrection from the dead at the last day.
right_choice: He rose in the same body, uncorrupted, declared Himself God's Son, and vanquished death as Head of His Church.
wrong_choices: He took a new glorified body unlike the one that suffered and died on the cross. | He appeared spiritually to the disciples but His actual body remained in the tomb eternally. | He rose to vindication but remained subordinate to the Father's authority in the heavens.
basis_note: Acts 2:27 says he did not see decay; Luke 24:39 shows a risen body of flesh and bones; Rom 1:4 and 4:25 show him declared Son of God and raised for justification; 1 Cor 15:20-22 shows him as firstfruits.
audit_why: The right choice was too long and said Christ "became" Head of the Church, when the catechism says he rose as the head; it is now shorter and matches the catechism, and the reference is tidied.

question: How was Christ exalted in his ascension?
answer: Christ was exalted in his ascension, in that having after his resurrection often appeared unto and conversed with his apostles, speaking to them of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God, and giving them commission to preach the gospel to all nations, forty days after his resurrection, he, in our nature, and as our head, triumphing over enemies, visibly went up into the highest heavens, there to receive gifts for men, to raise up our affections thither, and to prepare a place for us, where himself is, and shall continue till his second coming at the end of the world.
right_choice: After forty days appearing and commissioning apostles to preach, He visibly ascended to highest heavens as our head, triumphing to prepare a place for us.
wrong_choices: He went to heaven to await the final resurrection of the dead and end of the world. | He ascended to continue His mediatorial work in heaven entirely, separated from His earthly people. | He ascended spiritually but remained present on earth through His Spirit dwelling in believers.
basis_note: The verses show the forty days of appearances and teaching about the kingdom, the visible ascent into heaven, the commission to preach to all nations, the forerunner entering heaven, the preparing of a place, and heaven receiving Christ until the restoration.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: How is Christ exalted in his sitting at the right hand of God?
answer: Christ is exalted in his sitting at the right hand of God, in that as God-man he is advanced to the highest favor with God the Father, with all fulness of joy, glory, and power over all things in heaven and earth; and doth gather and defend his church, and subdue their enemies; furnisheth his ministers and people with gifts and graces, and maketh intercession for them.
right_choice: Christ at God's right hand has full power and glory, defends His church, furnishes gifts and graces, and intercedes for us.
wrong_choices: Christ continues in His humiliation, hiding His glory and submitting to the rule of earthly powers and Satan. | Christ rules only over the invisible church in heaven, having no authority or involvement with earthly matters and governments. | Christ waits passively in heaven until the day of judgment, performing no active work on behalf of His people.
verses: Philippians 2:9; Psalms 16:11; Psalms 110:1; Ephesians 1:22; Ephesians 4:11-12; Romans 8:34
basis_note: God exalts Christ to the highest place (Phil 2:9), gives Him power over all things and headship for the church (Eph 1:22), makes enemies His footstool (Ps 110:1), gives ministers (Eph 4:11-12), intercedes (Rom 8:34), and fills Him with joy (Ps 16:11).
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The teaching and wrong choices all check out against the verses, but the reference list used periods instead of the standard "Book Chapter:Verse" citation style, so it was reformatted for consistency.

question: How doth Christ make intercession?
answer: Christ maketh intercession, by his appearing in our nature continually before the Father in heaven, in the merit of his obedience and sacrifice on earth, declaring his will to have it applied to all believers; answering all accusations against them, and procuring for them quiet of conscience, notwithstanding daily failings, access with boldness to the throne of grace, and acceptance of their persons and services.
right_choice: By appearing in our nature before the Father, presenting his merit and sacrifice, and answering accusations against believers.
wrong_choices: By offering Himself again and again as a sacrifice for believers' sins in heaven. | By sending the Holy Spirit to plead believers' case and intercede for them before God. | By making our works acceptable before the Father's judgment and presenting our merits to God.
basis_note: Christ entered heaven to appear before God on our behalf (Heb 9:24), interceding for us (Rom 8:34), as our advocate for sins (1 John 2:1-2), so we approach the throne of grace with confidence (Heb 4:16).
audit_why: One wrong choice (Christ praying for believers) is actually true, as John 17 shows, so it was replaced with a clearly false one based on Hebrews 9:25, and the right choice was shortened to fit. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and choices are sound, but the reference list mixed in several verses (like John 3:16 and Eph 1:6) that do not actually support this specific answer about Christ's intercession, so it was narrowed to the five verses that do.

question: How is Christ to be exalted in his coming again to judge the world?
answer: Christ is to be exalted in his coming again to judge the world, in that he, who was unjustly judged and condemned by wicked men, shall come again at the last day in great power, and in the full manifestation of his own glory, and of his Father's, with all his holy angels, with a loud command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God, to judge the world in righteousness.
right_choice: Christ shall come at the last day in great power and glory, with His holy angels, to judge the world in righteousness.
wrong_choices: Christ shall return only in the hearts of believers through the work of the Holy Spirit, not in bodily form. | Christ shall come in humility and meekness, not in power and glory, to call all people to repentance and faith. | Christ shall come secretly and invisibly to rapture His church away before the world's destruction and final judgment.
reference: Acts 3:14-15; Matt 24:30; Luke 9:26; Matt 25:31; 1 Thess 4:16; Acts 17:31
verses: Acts 3:14-15; Matt 24:30; Luke 9:26; Matt 25:31; 1 Thess 4:16; Acts 17:31
basis_note: The answer is drawn from the question's proof texts: Christ was rejected by men (Acts 3:14-15), returns in power and glory with angels (Matt 24:30; Luke 9:26; Matt 25:31), with a command, archangel's voice and trumpet (1 Thess 4:16), to judge in righteousness (Acts 17:31).
audit_why: The answer and choices are sound, but one reference, Matthew 14:30 (Peter sinking), was a slip for Matthew 24:30, which speaks of the Son of Man coming in power and glory, so I corrected it. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer borrowed KJV wording ('with a shout, with the voice of the archangel') instead of the BSB's 'with a loud command, with the voice of an archangel'; this has been corrected to match the BSB text of 1 Thessalonians 4:16, with the rest of the question, right answer, wrong choices, and reference left unchanged as they already hold up under the cited verses.

question: What benefits has Christ procured by His mediation?
answer: Christ, by His mediation, has procured redemption, with all other benefits of the covenant of grace.
right_choice: Christ, by His mediation, has procured redemption, with all other benefits of the covenant of grace.
wrong_choices: Christ, by His mediation, has procured salvation for all people without exception, whether or not they believe. | Christ, by His mediation, has procured earthly wealth and health for all who follow Him. | Christ, by His mediation, has procured only the forgiveness of past sins, with no other benefits of the covenant.
basis_note: Hebrews 9:12 says Christ entered once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption. 2 Corinthians 1:20 says all God's promises are "Yes" in Christ, which supports the wider "all other benefits of the covenant."
audit_why: The old-style "hath" was changed to "has", and the wrong choices were replaced with ones that are clearly wrong (one of them was also a true benefit of Christ) and match the right answer in form.

question: How do we come to be made partakers of the benefits which Christ hath procured?
answer: We are made partakers of the benefits which Christ hath procured, by the application of them unto us, which is the work especially of God the Holy Ghost.

question: Who are made partakers of redemption through Christ?
answer: Redemption is certainly applied and effectually communicated to all those for whom Christ has purchased it; in time they are enabled by the Holy Spirit to believe in Christ according to the gospel.
right_choice: Those for whom Christ purchased redemption, who are enabled by the Holy Spirit to believe the gospel.
wrong_choices: Those who are baptized and remain members of the visible church, sharing in its sacraments throughout their lives. | Those who faithfully keep the moral law, produce good works, and demonstrate their worthiness through righteous living. | All people universally, since Christ's redemption is offered to all and none are excluded from the possibility of salvation.
basis_note: Christ lays down His life for His sheep, and everyone the Father gives Him comes to Him; faith itself is the gift of God. The answer follows from these verses.
audit_why: The answer used older wording ("hath", "Holy Ghost"), so it now says "has" and "Holy Spirit" as the BSB does; one wrong choice came too close to the catechism's own teaching on the elect, so it was replaced with a clearly wrong one.

question: Can they who have never heard the gospel, and so know not Jesus Christ, nor believe in him, be saved by their living according to the light of nature?
answer: They who, having never heard the gospel, know not Jesus Christ, and believe not in him, cannot be saved, be they never so diligent to frame their lives according to the light of nature, or the laws of that religion which they profess; neither is there salvation in any other, but in Christ alone, who is the Savior only of his body the church.
right_choice: No; salvation is in Christ alone, however diligently they live by the light of nature or their own religion.
wrong_choices: Yes, if they follow the moral law written on their hearts and live righteously before God. | Yes, if they respond to God's revelation in nature and act on the light they receive. | No, but God ensures that all people eventually hear the gospel message before they die.
basis_note: Acts 4:12 says salvation is in no one else and no other name, and Romans 10:14 says people cannot believe in one they have not heard. Together they teach that unhearing people cannot be saved by light of nature.
audit_why: The catechism's teaching is right and the Bible verses support it (Acts 4:12, Rom 10:14, John 8:24), but the right choice was worded differently from the others, so I made it open with "No" and follow the catechism's own wording.

question: Are all they saved who hear the gospel, and live in the church?
answer: All that hear the gospel, and live in the visible church, are not saved; but they only who are true members of the church invisible.
right_choice: Not all who hear the gospel and live in the visible church are saved, but only true members of the invisible church.
wrong_choices: Yes. All baptized members of the visible church and their children are certainly saved by its grace. | Yes. But some who are saved may lose their salvation through unfaithfulness and later unbelief. | No. Many are saved outside the visible church through other religions and sincere moral living.
basis_note: Romans 9:6 says not all descended from Israel are Israel, and Matthew 7:21 says not everyone who calls Jesus Lord will enter the kingdom. Together they teach that outward church membership does not guarantee salvation.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What is the visible church?
answer: The visible church is a society made up of all such as in all ages and places of the world do profess the true religion, and of their children.

question: What are the special privileges of the visible church?
answer: The visible church has the privilege of being under God's special care and government; of being protected and preserved in all ages, notwithstanding the opposition of all enemies; and of enjoying the communion of saints, the ordinary means of salvation, and offers of grace by Christ to all its members in the ministry of the gospel, testifying that whoever believes in Him will be saved, and excluding none who come to Him.
right_choice: God's special care and protection, communion of saints, means of salvation, and gospel offers excluding none who come.
wrong_choices: Authority to forgive sins on God's behalf, power to mediate salvation, and governance over conscience. | Certainty of salvation for all members, special revelations from heaven, and direct divine guidance. | Exemption from persecution and suffering, material blessings, and protection from all worldly troubles and harm.
basis_note: Scripture shows God covering and shielding Zion (Isa 4:5-6; Isa 31:5), the believers' fellowship and ministry (Acts 2:42; Eph 4:11-12), the gospel promising salvation to believers (Mark 16:16), and none who come to Christ turned away (John 6:37).
audit_why: The catechism answer and the wrong choices are sound, but the right choice was too long, so I shortened it to match the catechism's teaching. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The checked verses (Isa 4:5; Isa 31:5; Acts 2:42; Mark 16:16; John 6:37) still support the answer and wrong choices as given, but the answer's wording used archaic terms like 'hath' and 'whosoever' instead of the BSB's modern phrasing, so it was reworded to modern English while keeping the same meaning.

question: What is the invisible church?
answer: The invisible church is the whole number of the elect, that have been, are, or shall be gathered into one under Christ the head.
right_choice: The invisible church is the whole number of the elect, that have been, are, or shall be gathered into one under Christ the head.
wrong_choices: The invisible church is all who profess the true religion in the world, together with their children. | The invisible church is the sum of all believers who have reached heaven; they continue to intercede for the living. | The invisible church is every person who has ever lived; God knows and preserves all for final judgment.
basis_note: John 11:52 speaks of God's scattered children gathered together into one, and Ephesians 1:22-23 names Christ as head over the church, which is His body. Together they teach the answer's content.
audit_why: One wrong choice nearly restated the catechism's teaching about true believers within the visible church, so it was replaced with the catechism's definition of the visible church, which is clearly wrong here.

question: What special benefits do the members of the invisible church enjoy by Christ?
answer: The members of the invisible church by Christ enjoy union and communion with him in grace and glory.
right_choice: Union and communion with him in grace and glory.
wrong_choices: The members of the invisible church enjoy freedom from all temptation and sin; they are guaranteed never to fall from grace. | The members of the invisible church enjoy special privileges and authority; they govern the visible church through its leaders. | The members of the invisible church enjoy the ministry, oracles, and ordinances of God; they receive these only through the visible church.
basis_note: Believers are made alive, raised, and seated with Christ by grace (Eph 2:5-6), and Christ wills that they be with Him and see His glory (John 17:24). Union, communion, grace, and glory are taught together.
audit_why: The catechism's answer is union and communion with Christ in grace and glory, but one wrong choice (assurance and fellowship) was too close to that, so I replaced it with a choice that describes the visible church's outward privileges.

question: What is that union which the elect have with Christ?
answer: The union which the elect have with Christ is the work of God's grace, whereby they are spiritually and mystically, yet really and inseparably, joined to Christ as their head and husband; which is done in their effectual calling.
right_choice: God's grace whereby the elect are joined to Christ as head and husband in their effectual calling
wrong_choices: The work of Christ's power whereby believers overcome sin and death through faith in his resurrection | God's grace whereby the elect are bound to obey Christ's moral law in all their actions | The spiritual joining of all believers to Christ through baptism and the Lord's Supper
basis_note: Believers are one with the Lord in spirit, Christ is head of the church as husband is of wife, none can snatch them from His hand, they are called into fellowship with His Son, and salvation is by grace as God's gift.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What is effectual calling?
answer: Effectual calling is the work of God's almighty power and grace, whereby (out of his free and special love to his elect, and from nothing in them moving him thereunto ) he doth, in his accepted time, invite and draw them to Jesus Christ, by his word and Spirit; savingly enlightening their minds, renewing and powerfully determining their wills, so as they (although in themselves dead in sin) are hereby made willing and able freely to answer his call, and to accept and embrace the grace offered and conveyed therein.

question: Are the elect only effectually called?
answer: All the elect, and they only, are effectually called; although others may be, and often are, outwardly called by the ministry of the word, and have some common operations of the Spirit; who, for their wilful neglect and contempt of the grace offered to them, being justly left in their unbelief, do never truly come to Jesus Christ.
right_choice: All the elect, and only they, are effectually called; others may be outwardly called but never truly come to Christ
wrong_choices: Only the elect are outwardly called; all who are effectually called must have heard the gospel. | All who hear the gospel are effectively called; some respond and come to Christ, others resist willfully. | All people are equally called by the word and Spirit; only the elect choose to come to Christ.
basis_note: Acts 13:48 says those appointed to eternal life believe, Matthew 22:14 says many are called but few chosen, and Matthew 13:20-21 and Hebrews 6:4-6 describe those who receive the word but fall away. Psalm 81:11-12 shows God giving over those who refuse to listen.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What is the communion in grace which the members of the invisible church have with Christ?
answer: The communion in grace which the members of the invisible church have with Christ, is their partaking of the virtue of his mediation, in their justification, adoption, sanctification, and whatever else, in this life, manifests their union with him.
right_choice: Partaking of the virtue of Christ's mediation in justification, adoption, sanctification, and whatever manifests union with him
wrong_choices: Keeping the commandments of Christ perfectly in this life, so as to earn a place with him in glory. | Sharing in the divine nature of Christ, so as to become partakers of his Godhead and his eternal Sonship. | Being outwardly joined to Christ by baptism and by sharing in the Lord's Supper with the visible church.
basis_note: Believers are "in Christ Jesus," and He is their righteousness (justification), holiness (sanctification), and redemption; Ephesians 1:5 adds adoption through Jesus Christ.
audit_why: The right answer follows the catechism, but the three wrong choices described the same blessings in other words, so I replaced them with choices that clearly differ from the catechism's teaching.

question: What is justification?
answer: Justification is an act of God's free grace unto sinners, in which he pardoneth all their sins, accepteth and accounteth their persons righteous in his sight; not for any thing wrought in them, or done by them, but only for the perfect obedience and full satisfaction of Christ, by God imputed to them, and received by faith alone.

question: How is justification an act of God's free grace?
answer: Although Christ, by his obedience and death, did make a proper, real, and full satisfaction to God's justice in the behalf of them that are justified; yet inasmuch as God accepteth the satisfaction from a surety, which he might have demanded of them, and did provide this surety, his own only Son, imputing his righteousness to them, and requiring nothing of them for their justification but faith, which also is his gift, their justification is to them of free grace.
right_choice: Christ made full satisfaction for the justified; God accepts it from a surety and imputes Christ's righteousness, requiring only faith
wrong_choices: Christ made satisfaction sufficient for all; God accepts personal righteousness from those who have faith and obedience. | Christ made full satisfaction through the law; God accepts human effort from believers and imputes faith as righteousness. | Christ made partial satisfaction for the justified; God accepts works with faith and imputes sanctification for justification.
basis_note: Romans 3:24 says we are justified freely by God's grace through Christ's redemption; Romans 8:32 shows God giving His Son; 2 Corinthians 5:21 shows imputed righteousness; Ephesians 2:8 says faith is God's gift.
audit_why: No fault found.

question: What is justifying faith?
answer: Justifying faith is a saving grace, wrought in the heart of a sinner by the Spirit and word of God, whereby he, being convinced of his sin and misery, and of the disability in himself and all other creatures to recover him out of his lost condition, not only assenteth to the truth of the promise of the gospel, but receiveth and resteth upon Christ and his righteousness, therein held forth, for pardon of sin, and for the accepting and accounting of his person righteous in the sight of God for salvation.
right_choice: Saving grace wrought by Spirit and word; conviction of sin and misery; receiving and resting on Christ and his righteousness for pardon
wrong_choices: Divine grace wrought by the Spirit alone; rejection of sin; believing in Christ's person and work for salvation. | Transforming grace wrought by sacraments and preaching; repentance from sin; personal effort combined with Christ for pardon. | Intellectual assent to the gospel wrought by the word; understanding of sin; acceptance of Christian doctrine for salvation.
verses: Ephesians 1:13; John 1:12; Philippians 3:9; Acts 10:43; Acts 2:37; Ephesians 2:1
basis_note: No single verse gives the full definition, but together they teach it: hearing and believing the gospel by the Spirit (Eph 1:13), receiving Christ for forgiveness and righteousness (John 1:12, Phil 3:9, Acts 10:43), convicted of sin (Acts 2:37), and dead in sins (Eph 2:1).
audit_why: No fault found.

question: How does faith justify a sinner in the sight of God?
answer: Faith justifies a sinner in the sight of God, not because of the other graces that always accompany it, or because of good works that are its fruits, nor because the grace of faith or any act of it is credited to him for his justification; but only because it is the instrument by which he receives and applies Christ and His righteousness.
right_choice: Faith justifies not as good works or faith itself imputed, but as instrument to receive and apply Christ's righteousness
wrong_choices: Good works justify through faith, with faith itself the instrument God uses to impute Christ's obedience. | Faith justifies because believers receive Christ and apply their own righteousness through the power of the Holy Spirit. | Faith justifies because it is itself the gift of God's righteousness imputed and accounted to believers for salvation.
reference: Gal 3:11; Rom 3:28; Rom 4:5; Rom 10:10; John 1:12; Phil 3:9; Gal 2:16
basis_note: Paul rejects a righteousness from the law and receives the righteousness that comes through faith in Christ, justified by faith apart from works. The word "instrument" is the catechism's own summary of this.
doubt: Romans 4:5 says faith itself "is credited as righteousness," which sits uneasily with the answer's denial that the act of faith is credited, so the answer reads "faith" there as the means of receiving Christ.
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The catechism's teaching and all three wrong choices remain correctly wrong under the listed verses, but the wording used archaic KJV terms ('doth', 'receiveth', 'thereof') out of step with the site's BSB style, so it was reworded into modern English without changing its meaning.

question: What is adoption?
answer: Adoption is an act of the free grace of God, in and for his only Son Jesus Christ, whereby all those that are justified are received into the number of his children, have his name put upon them, the Spirit of his Son given to them, are under his fatherly care and dispensations, admitted to all the liberties and privileges of the sons of God, made heirs of all the promises, and fellow heirs with Christ in glory.

question: What is sanctification?
answer: Sanctification is a work of God's grace, whereby they whom God hath, before the foundation of the world, chosen to be holy, are in time, through the powerful operation of his Spirit applying the death and resurrection of Christ unto them, renewed in their whole man after the image of God; having the seeds of repentance unto life, and all other saving graces, put into their hearts, and those graces so stirred up, increased, and strengthened, as that they more and more die unto sin, and rise unto newness of life.

question: What is repentance unto life?
answer: Repentance unto life is a saving grace, wrought in the heart of a sinner by the Spirit and word of God, whereby, out of the sight and sense, not only of the danger, but also of the filthiness and odiousness of his sins, and upon the apprehension of God's mercy in Christ to such as are penitent, he so grieves for and hates his sins, as that he turns from them all to God, purposing and endeavoring constantly to walk with him in all the ways of new obedience.

question: Wherein do justification and sanctification differ?
answer: Although sanctification be inseparably joined with justification, yet they differ, in that God in justification imputeth the righteousness of Christ; in sanctification his Spirit infuseth grace, and enableth to the exercise thereof; in the former, sin is pardoned; in the other, it is subdued: the one doth equally free all believers from the revenging wrath of God, and that perfectly in this life, that they never fall into condemnation; the other is neither equal in all, nor in this life perfect in any, but growing up to perfection.
right_choice: Justification imputes Christ's righteousness, pardons sin, perfectly frees from wrath; sanctification infuses grace, subdues sin, grows but never perfect
wrong_choices: Justification and sanctification both impute righteousness, both completely free from sin, both perfect in this life for believers. | Justification frees from guilt; sanctification removes sinful nature completely; both are unequal in believers and never finished. | Justification pardons sin gradually through faith; sanctification immediately frees from wrath and infuses perfect holiness eternally.
